item.title: 3 tourists die while bathing at Himchhari beach in Cox’s Bazar, 2 missing
item.description:
Three tourists have died while swimming at Himchhari beach in Cox's Bazar and two others are missing today, Wednesday, around 4: 30 PM at the beach adjacent to the museum of Marina Resort on the Cox's Bazar-Teknaf Marine Drive in Himchhari.

Fire service, lifeguards, and beach workers conducted a search until 7: 30 PM but couldn't find the two missing individuals.

According to police and lifeguard sources, a group of 12 people from Dhaka went to visit Himchhari beach.

Among them, five people went swimming in the sea. At that time, due to a large wave, all five got submerged. Later, lifeguards and locals rescued three of them. However, by then, they had already passed away. Searches are ongoing to find the other two missing individuals.

The three deceased tourists are Md Borhan (23), Saiful Islam (23), and Nafisul Haque (22) from Diabari, Uttara, Dhaka. Their bodies have been taken from Himchhari to the morgue at Cox's Bazar Sadar Hospital at night.

The the incident has been confirmed by the Officer-in-Charge (OC) of Ramu Police Station, AK Fazlul Haque. He told Prothom Alo that operations are ongoing to rescue the two missing individuals.

Imtiaz Ahmed, regional director of the private lifeguard company Sea-Safe, told Prothom Alo that the group of 12 tourists from Dhaka went to the beach adjacent to the museum of Marina Resort in Himchhari, about 9 kilometers south of the city, around 4 PM. Among them, five went swimming in the sea. When they got submerged due to waves, lifeguards and locals quickly initiated rescue efforts. Three were rescued but had already died.

Imtiaz Ahmed stated that from Kolatoli to Laboni Point along the Cox's Bazar sea beach, about five kilometers, Sea-Safe has 27 lifeguards available for rescue operations if someone goes missing while swimming.

However, there aren't enough personnel to conduct rescue operations along the vast stretch of beach from Kolatoli to the south, including Dariyanagar, Himchhari, Patuartek, Inani, and Teknaf.

Imtiaz Ahmed added that over 300,000 tourists are currently in Cox's Bazar. This afternoon, a large crowd gathered at Laboni Point for the immersion festival of idols. Seeing the crowd at various points on the beach, many people are rushing to swim at Dariyanagar and Himchhari beaches, which is increasing the risk of accidents.

According to Imtiaz Ahmed, at least 20 hidden channels have formed at Kolatoli, Sugandha, and Laboni Points, including Himchhari-Dariyanagar. Despite multiple places displaying red flags warning against swimming in dangerous areas, many are not adhering to the warnings.

Currently, more than 300, 000 tourists are staying in Cox''s Bazar. It has been reported by the concerned individuals that no rooms are available in any of the over 500 hotels, guesthouses, resorts, and cottages.
Most recently, on September 27 at Laboni Point on Cox''s Bazar beach, a tourist died from being swept away by the sea.

item.title: Rashid leads Afghanistan rout as Bangladesh crumble for 160
item.description:
Parvez Hossain scored a fighting 70, but Bangladesh were bowled out for 160 in 40 overs against Afghanistan in their must-win match of the tri-nation One Day International series at Sheikh Zayed Stadium in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday.

Leg-spinner Rashid Khan led Afghanistan’s bowling attack with four wickets for 31 runs, including two wickets in consecutive deliveries to wrap up Bangladesh’s innings.

Bangladesh, who elected to bat first, needed to beat Afghanistan by at least 41 runs to qualify for the final. Their hopes now depend on restricting Afghanistan to a sufficiently low total.

Bangladesh suffered an early collapse, losing four wickets for just 28 runs. Tanzid Hasan fell to Yamin Ahmadzai before Soumya Sarkar was bowled off the next ball, leaving the side in deep trouble.

Najmul Hossain offered some resistance with 15 off 23 balls but was caught behind, while captain Towhid Hridoy fell to Azmatullah Omarzai, who took a return catch.

With Bangladesh struggling at 28 for four in the seventh over, Parvez and Saif Hassan came together to rebuild the innings. The pair added 92 runs for the fifth wicket, helping Bangladesh cross 100 after 26 overs.

Parvez reached his half-century off 74 balls, scoring his second ODI fifty after being included in the squad for the tri-series as a replacement for Litton Das.

Saif, however, fell immediately after Parvez reached the milestone, attempting a big shot against Mohammad Nabi and offering a catch to Nangeyalia Kharote at midwicket. He scored 41 off 82 balls.

Mehidy Hasan Miraz lasted just seven deliveries before being caught at backward square leg off Bilal Sami for two.

Parvez continued to fight, bringing up Bangladesh’s 150 with a six off Nabi in the 39th over. But Rashid struck again, bowling Shoriful Islam for seven before trapping Parvez leg-before-wicket for 70 off 96 balls, an innings featuring five fours and two sixes.

Rashid then dismissed debutant Aliss Al Islam, caught by Nabi at slip, before Mustafizur Rahman was bowled first ball. Bangladesh lost their final three wickets in quick succession to finish on 160.

item.title: Tk2,811cr spent, no buses run as govt scraps Gazipur BRT
item.description:
The decision, taken at a cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Sunday, means stations and concrete lane dividers built along the airport-Gazipur corridor will now be demolished, potentially adding to the project’s enormous financial losses.
A Road Transport and Highways Division letter issued on Monday directed the authorities to convert the roughly 20km corridor into a regular three-to-six-lane highway and eventually widen two flyovers from two to four lanes.
The government will also dissolve Dhaka Bus Rapid Transit Company Limited, established to operate the service, and transfer its activities to the Roads and Highways Department.
The authorities have been given 15 days to report progress on the closure process, including resolving legal complications with development partners.
Launched in 2012 under the Awami League government, the project was originally estimated to cost Tk2,040 crore and scheduled for completion in 2016.
Three revisions pushed the cost to Tk4,268 crore. A further proposal last year sought Tk6,598 crore and an extension until 2029, but it was not approved.
The project was designed to carry around 25,000 passengers daily in dedicated bus lanes. Instead, construction narrowed one of the country’s busiest highways, causing years of congestion and hardship.
Seven people also died in construction-related accidents.
A BUET expert panel, led by Prof Samsul Haque, recommended cancellation, describing the project as a case of systemic failure involving faulty design, weak technical scrutiny and poor coordination.
“Even if the BRT buses were launched, Gazipur residents could only travel up to the airport and would then have to change buses again, which is not practical,” Samsul told Dhaka Tribune.
The panel also called for accountability among consultants, officials and agencies involved in the project.
However, cancellation could bring further costs. The Bangladesh Institute of Planners previously estimated that dismantling infrastructure and compensating contractors could exceed Tk1,000 crore.
A Gazipur-based citizens’ platform opposes the decision, arguing that 97% of construction is complete.
Its president, Md Shamsul Haque, said the group would formally protest the cancellation.
For commuters who have endured 14 years of disruption, the promised rapid bus service will now remain a project that never carried a passenger.

item.title: Who are the women powering India’s youth-led ‘Cockroach’ protests?
item.description:
On July 20, Navkiran Natt and her partner set out for the magistrate’s office in New Delhi to get married. They arrived to find a tense situation, with police gathering to break up a youth-led march on Parliament. Office staff — and the couple’s wedding witnesses — were running late due to barricades.
The protest movement known as the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) had announced the march to demand the resignation of India’s then-Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The protesters were met with heavy resistance from security forces, who had deployed batons, tear gas and pellet-firing shotguns, leading to injuries and mass detentions.
Less than three months later, on October 10, Natt left home early in the morning and spent the day crisscrossing the locked-down Indian capital looking for a protest she could join.
“The success of this protest is not how many people will reach Jantar Mantar,” she told DW, referring to the protest site in central New Delhi. “It’s that even after all this barricading and state violence, people are leaving their homes to join.”
The CJP began as a satirical online movement after the chief justice of India, Surya Kant, referred to unemployed young people as “cockroaches” in an offhand remark. The name is an ironic riff on the name of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
After succeeding in seeing Pradhan step down in late July, the CJP is now demanding the resignation of the country’s controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after more than 130 million names were removed from draft electoral rolls nationwide.
With CJP leadership in judicial custody or under threat of detention, one name has fast become synonymous with the demonstrations: student leader Neha Bora, who prefers to use the pronoun they/them.
Bora has run through the streets to dodge police officials, climbed barricades in the face of security personnel, shouted slogans from detention vans and addressed press conferences alongside CJP spokespersons and others.
They are the president of the All India Students’ Association, the student wing of the Communist Party of India (Marxist–Leninist) Liberation (CPI-ML).
“In extremely disappointing, fearful, tyrannical times, people try to gather hope from whatever source they can … If these people are fighting, then probably we can also fight,” Bora told DW.
“It is a responsibility that you owe to people,” they added.
The Cockroach-led demonstrations also come at a time when women and members of the LGBTQ+ community are calling for greater autonomy for women in the aftermath of the gang rape of a 17-year-old girl in New Delhi in late September, placing the issue of safety in India back into the spotlight.
According to the National Crime Records Bureau, 441,534 cases of crimes against women were registered in 2024, averaging 1,210 cases per day. Experts say these official statistics can only give a partial account of gendered violence.
But despite facing sexualized backlash from police on the streets and from online mobs, the women and genderqueer people leading the movement reject being cast as victims.
“The “beti bachao” [save the daughter] thing just doesn’t cut it with this generation. It is a very specific ask: see us as political beings, free beings,” activist Kavita Krishnan told DW.
“Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao” (Save the Daughter, Educate the Daughter) is a flagship BJP government program launched in 2015.
These days, Gurmehar Kaur’s day starts like any other — a workout or a yoga class — and often ends with Indian Youth Congress’ lawyers getting her released from police detention.
“Resistance can’t be a separate event … a big day, and then you go back to your regular life,” she told DW.
The 29-year-old author of “The Young and the Restless: Youth and Politics in India” spent a better part of the last decade in the public eye.
This year, she joined the youth wing of India’s main opposition party, The Congress, whose offices are located a stone’s throw away from Jantar Mantar, the hub of the last wave of protests.
Kaur said her political association has given her access to resources that can support the movement, offering a safety net for protesters “regardless of their political affiliation.”
At a time when authorities are cracking down on CJP protesters, she said opposition members like her have a duty to fulfill: “Show up, put your body on the line.”
But showing up often comes with a cost, especially for women and queer protesters.
Kaur explained how male colleagues often “feel quite elated when their photos are in the media.” However, for her, “attention is equal to death and rape threats and humiliation and abuse.”
Navkiran Natt, an activist most significantly associated with the 2020–2021 farmers’ protests, echoes Kaur’s experience.
“If a woman is leading the protest, the first attack is on her sexuality,” she said.
Social media images have shown women protesters with their clothes torn during clashes with police.
Delhi officials have denied allegations of manhandling, adding that women protesters were treated with “dignity.”
Student leader Bora refuted the police’s claim, saying that a small number of female personnel were available to handle a large number of female protesters.
“Several women protesters came to protect me and prevent me from getting detained,” they said.
Authorities have registered a police case against a journalist who accused a senior Delhi police officer of sexual harassment under an Indian law meant to prevent crimes against members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. They say her own allegations are under investigation.
The internet was also flooded with AI-made, sexualized images of women protesters edited into protest photos.
This has not prevented protesters from taking to the streets even the day after being detained by authorities.
“They don’t know what they’re dealing with,” activist Krishnan said, referring to the government’s crackdown on demonstrators.
She said authorities assume sexual humiliation will scare women off, but “this is not a generation that thinks of… sexual violence as being something shameful.”
She was at the forefront of demonstrations after the 2012 “Nirbhaya” gang rape, where slogans like “Hang the rapists” were seen in public. This time, however, she said the anger “is not going to be about masculine displays of honor.”
It is about “dignity and freedom ... Women face all kinds of problems in every country, and Indian women are no different,” she added.
Krishnan said the youth-led protests are part of a wider global wave of “civilizational, cultural nationalism,” which uses gender and the language of protection, whether of daughters, families or tradition, to rally support against minorities, immigrants and trans people.
“You listen to the rhetoric of Donald Trump or Viktor Orban or the Alternative for Germany (AfD). It is the same,” she said, referring to politics in the United States and Europe. “If you look at what’s happening in India, you may be able to better understand what’s happening in your country.”
These young Indians, she said, are refusing to be taken in. They are “fighting back for a language of the future, a language that has hope.”

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,205 as one die in 24 hours
item.description:
One child died with measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours ending at 8am on Wednesday, bringing the country’s combined tally of confirmed and suspected measles-related deaths to 1,205 this year.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) classified the latest fatality as the suspected measles death.
With this, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,101, while confirmed deaths from measles have remained the same at 104.
A total of 997 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24-hour period, taking the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to 216,765.
Meanwhile, 13 new confirmed measles cases were recorded, pushing laboratory-confirmed infections to 23,212.
Since March 15 this year, a total of 192,695 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalised across the country, of whom 185,110 have recovered, according to the DGHS.

item.title: Harmony: Diplomatic community joins Durga Puja celebrations in Bangladesh
item.description:
Members of the diplomatic community in Bangladesh joined Durga Puja celebrations at temples and pandals in Dhaka and beyond, extending greetings to the Hindu community and highlighting the country’s rich cultural heritage, religious diversity and spirit of communal harmony.
The Hindu community says participation of members of the diplomatic community in this year’s festivities underscored the importance of cultural engagement and respect for religious diversity in Bangladesh, where festivals play a vital role in strengthening social bonds and promoting understanding among communities.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has said all citizens of Bangladesh enjoy equal rights regardless of their religious identity, stressing that being Bangladeshi matters more than belonging to a majority or minority community.
“Majority or minority is not the issue. The only thing that matters is that you are Bangladeshi,” he said while visiting the JM Sen Hall puja mandap in the port city on the occasion of Durga Puja on Tuesday, noting that people of different faiths fought together in the 1971 War of Liberation without distinguishing between Muslims, Hindus, Buddhists and Christians.
Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi took part in celebrations at several venues across the capital, including Jagannath Hall at the University of Dhaka, Dhakeshwari National Temple, Ramna Kali Mandir and the Gulshan-Banani Sarbajanin Puja Foundation.
He exchanged greetings with devotees, students and organisers, sharing in the festive spirit of the occasion. Sharadiya Durga Puja concludes today (Wednesday) with Bijoya Dashami.
On Maha Ashtami, Trivedi inaugurated the distribution of Mahaprasad at Dhakeshwari National Temple. He visited the Durga Puja pandal at Uttara Sarbojanin Temple and joined devotees in observing the festival.
Deputy High Commissioner Pawan Badhe also attended the Aarti Competition at Dhakeshwari Temple, where performers of different age groups presented the traditional Dhanuchi dance to the rhythmic beats of the dhak.
Other diplomatic missions also conveyed their greetings and joined the festivities, celebrating the traditions and cultural vibrancy of Bangladesh’s Hindu community.
US Ambassador to Bangladesh Brent T. Christensen joined the celebrations at Sarbajanin Puja Mandap in Amlapara, sharing the warmth, colour and joy of the festivities with members of the Hindu community. He extended his greetings in Bengali, saying, “Sobaike Sharadiya Subeccha.”
Ambassador of Switzerland to Bangladesh Reto Renggli attended Durga Puja celebrations at the Kumudini Welfare Trust in Tangail, describing the festival as an important reflection of Bangladesh’s rich social, cultural and religious diversity.
The Royal Norwegian Embassy in Dhaka wished everyone a happy Durga Puja, expressing hope that the festival would serve as a reminder of the values of peace, harmony, inclusiveness and mutual respect that bring communities together.
“As people across Bangladesh come together to celebrate Durga Puja, we send our warmest wishes to all and hope the festival serves as a reminder of the values of peace, harmony, inclusiveness, and respect that bring communities together,” said the Embassy.
Norwegian Ambassador Håkon Arald Gulbrandsen, High Commissioner of Canada Ajit Singh, Ambassador of Sweden Nicolas Weeks and the Embassy colleagues joined the festivities and experienced the warmth, traditions, and vibrant cultural heritage that make Durga Puja such a special occasion. “May this festive season bring joy, peace, and prosperity to all.”
Swedish Ambassador Nicolas Weeks attended the Durga Puja celebrations in Banani, Dhaka, offering his greetings to the community.
"Wishing everyone a very Happy Durga Puja! In the spirit of inclusion, peace, and harmony, may this festival bring happiness and prosperity to all,” Ambassador Weeks said.
The Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, meanwhile, extended its warm wishes to the Hindu community in Bangladesh and around the world, hoping the festival would bring peace, happiness, harmony and prosperity.
The Embassy of France in Bangladesh also wished everyone celebrating a joyful and peaceful Durga Puja.
The Australian High Commission in Dhaka said they had the privilege of joining festivities across the country and experiencing the warmth and hospitality that make this celebration so special.
The High Commission said Durga Puja is a reflection of the power of culture to bring people together and strengthen connections across communities.
Durga Puja, the largest religious festival of Bangladesh’s Hindu community, is marked by days of worship, cultural performances and community gatherings at temples and temporary pandals across the country.
Beyond its religious significance, the festival offers an opportunity for people from different backgrounds to come together in a shared celebration of culture, tradition and coexistence.

item.title: Bride tortured, killed over wedding gifts in Sherpur
item.description:
A 20-year-old newlywed woman died at her husband’s home in Sherpur’s Nalitabari upazila early Wednesday, just six days after her marriage.
The deceased, Lima Akter, died at her husband’s home in Paikhatla village of Rupnarayankura union in the early hours of October 21.
Lima’s family alleged that she was tortured and killed over her in-laws’ dissatisfaction with the gifts and other items brought from her parental home for the wedding, reports Bangla Tribun.
Police detained her husband, Ekramul Haque, 22, and mother-in-law, Farida Begum, 50, for questioning.
Lima was the daughter of Saidul Islam of Majhiyail village in Dhara union of Mymensingh’s Haluaghat upazila. She married Ekramul on October 15 in a family-arranged ceremony, with the denmohor set at Tk1.7 lakh.
According to family members, Lima visited her parents’ home with her husband on Sunday and returned to her in-laws’ house on Tuesday afternoon.
Relatives said a dispute broke out between the couple after Lima’s in-laws expressed dissatisfaction with the gifts and other items brought from her parents’ home.
Lima’s family alleged that she was tortured at her in-laws’ house that night.
Around 3:00am, Ekramul called Lima’s brother-in-law, saying she had fallen ill. About an hour later, her in-laws took her to Nalitabari Upazila Health Complex, where doctors declared her dead.
Lima’s relatives said they noticed injury marks on her body at the hospital and informed police.
Police went to the hospital, took custody of the body and sent it for the necessary legal procedures.
Dr Fahad Rahman, resident medical officer at Nalitabari Upazila Health Complex, said Lima had died before she was brought to the hospital.
Lima’s relatives alleged that the dispute over the gifts escalated and that she was physically assaulted and strangled to death.
However, the exact cause of her death has not yet been established and will be determined through investigation and autopsy.
Ekramul, however, denied the allegations.
He said he went to sleep at night and woke up to find the door of their room open. He then went outside and found Lima hanging by her scarf from the sunshade of a nearby semi-pucca house.
He claimed that he brought her down and informed his brother about the incident.
Nalitabari police Sub-Inspector Abdul Hannan said injury marks were found on the victim’s body. Her husband, Ekramul Haque, and mother-in-law, Farida Begum, have been detained for questioning in connection with the incident.
The body has been sent to the Sherpur morgue for an autopsy to determine the exact cause of death.
Police said further details about the cause of death will be known after the autopsy report is received and the investigation is completed.

item.title: Dilip Agarwala placed on 4-day remand in July attempted murder case
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Wednesday placed Diamond World Managing Director Dilip Kumar Agarwala on a four-day remand in a case over an armed attack on protesters and the shooting of Abdur Zabbar in the Anti-Discrimination Student Movement in capital’s Uttara area in August 2024.
The court also granted him a one-day remand on Tuesday in a separate money laundering case filed with Gulshan Police.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Sarah Farzana Haque passed the order on Wednesday after hearing arguments from both sides.
Investigation officer and Uttara West police Sub-Inspector Md Sumon Mia produced Agarwala before the court and sought a 10-day remand for questioning.
State prosecutor Shamsuddoha Sumon argued in favour of the remand, alleging that Agarwala had financed the Awami League and served as a central leader of the party. He further alleged that Agarwala had worked to thwart the student movement and was involved in shooting protesters.
Defence lawyer Anwarul Kabir Babul opposed the remand and sought bail, arguing that Agarwala was abroad at the time of the incident and could not, therefore, have been involved.
The lawyer also said Agarwala had resigned from the Awami League five years earlier. He questioned the need for remand, noting that the case had been under investigation for a year without any evidence of Agarwala’s involvement being established.
After hearing both sides, the court granted a four-day remand.
According to the case documents, students and members of the public gathered peacefully beside BNS Centre on the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway in the Uttara West Police Station area on August 5, 2024, during the Anti-Discrimination Student Movement.
The accused allegedly launched an armed attack on the protesters and opened indiscriminate fire on the instructions of the prime accused and others.
A protester, identified as Abdur Jabbar in the case, was shot and sustained severe injuries to the lower part of his spine. He received prolonged treatment at Dhaka Medical College Hospital before filing the case with Uttara West Police Station on March 27, 2025, after recovering.
In the remand petition, the investigation officer said preliminary evidence suggested that Agarwala had been present at the scene and participated in the attack in collusion with other accused.
The officer said Agarwala needed to be interrogated to uncover the circumstances of the incident, recover the firearms allegedly used in the attack, identify other suspects and facilitate their arrest.
Agarwala is listed as the 31st accused in the case.
Earlier on Tuesday, a court granted him a one-day remand in a separate money laundering case involving allegations of trading gold and diamonds worth around Tk6,781.9 crore through smuggling.
Detective Branch (DB) police arrested him from the capital’s Gulshan area on October 19 in connection with that case.

item.title: Does Pakistan-Taliban conflict create a strategic opening for India?
item.description:
Pakistan and Afghanistan right now are locked in a cycle of escalating tension. Repeated border clashes have strained ties between the two nations.
The current round of tensions began in February 2026, when Pakistan launched strikes into Afghanistan targeting Taliban militants. At one point in March, Pakistan’s defense minister said the country was at “open war” with Afghanistan. Periodic bouts of violence have continued since then, with the latest Pakistani strikes targeting the Afghan Taliban’s “terrorist hubs” reported earlier in October.
At the heart of the dispute is Pakistan’s accusation that the Taliban authorities in Kabul allow the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant group, to target Pakistan from Afghan territory. Kabul denies providing the group with sanctuary.
As the two neighbors trade strikes, the escalating conflict “presents a significant diplomatic and strategic opportunity for India,” Shanthie Mariet D’Souza, an Afghanistan expert and founder of the India-based Mantraya Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.
D’Souza argues the confrontation has weakened Pakistan’s traditional influence in Afghanistan and encouraged the Taliban to broaden its external relations.
“India can respond by expanding diplomatic engagement, humanitarian assistance, development projects and trade, while seeking assurances that Afghan territory will not be used by anti-India militant groups,” she said.
However, D’Souza cautioned against interpreting the opening as a fundamental realignment.
“There is no ideological alignment between India and the Taliban,” she said. Afghanistan under Taliban rule is likely to pursue a diversified foreign policy rather than align exclusively with New Delhi.
India also lacks the geographical advantages, economic leverage and security presence needed to replace Pakistan’s influence, she notes. “The scenario of the Taliban becoming a strategic ally remains far-fetched.”
Former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan Amar Sinha warned against viewing the conflict simply as an opportunity for New Delhi to gain at Pakistan’s expense.
“The issues have very little to do with India,” Sinha told DW, arguing that India was not seeking strategic advantage from the fighting. He also pointed to the consequences of Pakistan’s military actions for Afghan civilians.
“Yet the rupture has made Kabul’s search for alternative partners more pressing,” he added.
For India, that creates an opening, but not necessarily a strategic alignment, Sinha notes. The Taliban can seek Indian assistance while maintaining relations with China, Russia, Iran and Gulf states, preserving its autonomy rather than exchanging dependence on Pakistan for dependence on India.
Gautam Mukhopadhyaya, another former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan, sees the deterioration in relations between Pakistan and the Taliban as an opportunity for India to recover some of the strategic ground it lost when the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
“The crisis has allowed strategic openings for India,” Mukhopadhyaya told DW. He warned, however, that New Delhi’s own treatment of Afghans could undermine its efforts to build a durable relationship.
He pointed to restrictions affecting Afghans seeking Indian visas for education, scholarships, work and medical treatment.
“For all practical purposes, India’s security establishment treats Afghans as proxy Pakistanis and ‘terrorists’ by default,” he said.
Former Afghan partners had been left “disappointed, even bitter,” Mukhopadhyaya added. “A strategic relationship built on the sands of oppression is not a sound foundation.”
India has restored air freight links between Kabul and Delhi and between Kabul and Amritsar in northwestern India in December 2025.
Bilateral trade between India and Afghanistan stood at about $908 million (€807 million) in the 2025-26 fiscal year, while trade between Pakistan and Afghanistan fell sharply amid repeated border closures.
On October 14, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi stressed the importance of relations with India during talks with Indian charge d’affaires Yatin Patel, signaling Kabul’s interest in expanding economic cooperation.
But air freight is expensive, and India cannot easily replace Pakistan as a transit route.
New Delhi has sought to use Iran’s Chabahar port to improve access to Afghanistan and Central Asia, but regional instability and complications surrounding Iran have constrained those ambitions.
D’Souza cautioned that “the ongoing conflict in Iran” limits India’s ability to use Chabahar as a crucial trade and connectivity hub.
Gulshan Sachdeva, a professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University specializing in Afghanistan and Eurasian connectivity, highlighted similar obstacles.
“In the last few decades, Islamabad has obstructed Kabul’s efforts to gain access to the vast Indian market. However, political instability in Afghanistan and sanctions on Iran have undermined these efforts,” Sachdeva told DW.
“Afghanistan’s potential as a connector between regional markets remains considerable, but the infrastructure and political conditions needed to realize it are far from assured,” he added.
Sachdeva also sees Russia and China as better positioned to shape Afghanistan’s wider economic integration. Alternative routes may become more attractive to India, but they are not commercially viable overnight.
Pakistan has portrayed arch-rival India’s growing engagement with the Taliban as a security threat. On October 7, Pakistani diplomat Muhammad Jawad Ajmal accused India at the United Nations of providing the Taliban with material and logistical support.
“Under the guise of humanitarian aid, they have been actively supporting the Taliban regime with material and logistical support for carrying out terrorist attacks against Pakistan,” Ajmal said.
The allegation reflects Islamabad’s position and has not been established as fact.
Pakistan has accused India of supporting the TTP and the Balochistan Liberation Army, a militant organization.
India rejects accusations of backing militant activity, while the Taliban denies allowing Afghan territory to be used for attacks against Pakistan.
Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani expert on military and security affairs at King’s College London, offered a more nuanced assessment of Pakistan’s position.
“India has stepped into a space and is trying to exert its influence and feed anti-Pakistan groups intelligence,” she told DW.
Siddiqa added that Pakistan’s establishment continues to view the crisis through “a singular security lens.”
“Islamabad feels physically squeezed from both sides,” she said, adding that closer Kabul-New Delhi ties could create “a dangerous two-front security trap” for Pakistan.
India may gain more room to operate in Afghanistan as ties between Kabul and Islamabad deteriorate. But the Taliban is unlikely to put all its eggs in New Delhi’s basket.

item.title: Biman to resume Riyadh flight on October 25 as security improves
item.description:
Biman Bangladesh Airlines will operate a flight to Riyadh on October 25 as the security situation in Saudi Arabia improves following attacks on airports.
The flight will depart Dhaka at 1:25am on October 26, Bangladesh time, the airline’s public relations department said on Wednesday. Further decisions on other Riyadh-bound flights will be made after assessing the overall security situation, Biman said.
Meanwhile, the airline resumed flights to Dammam on Wednesday. Until October 26, a daily flight will depart Dhaka for Dammam at 8:00am, Bangladesh time, using Boeing 777 aircraft.
For Jeddah, Biman will operate two flights from Dhaka on October 22, followed by one daily flight at 7:20pm on October 23, 24 and 25. Flights to Medina have been operating since October 18 using Boeing 787 aircraft. The route’s operations and schedule will remain unchanged until further notice.
Biman said it would provide updates on flight operations and schedules as decisions are made. Passengers have been advised to contact their nearest Biman sales centre for ticket purchases, bookings and other travel-related information.

item.title: Tourists urged to leave Sajek as road blockade resumes Thursday
item.description:
Tourists staying in Sajek have been urged to leave the area by Wednesday as the Sajek Gono Odhikar Rokkha Committee and Sajek Karbari Association have announced a fresh road blockade from Thursday over the non-implementation of their three-point demands.
The announcement was made in a joint statement issued around 4pm on Wednesday by Sajek Karbari Association President Notun Joy Chakma and Sajek Gono Odhikar Rokkha Committee Convener Babudhan Chakma.
The blockade had been suspended from Friday to Wednesday at the request of the Durga Puja celebration committees of Baghaichhari and Machalong markets to allow the Hindu community to celebrate its largest religious festival.
The two organizations initially enforced an indefinite road blockade on October 11. The programme was later relaxed twice following assurances from the administration.
However, the groups have announced a fresh blockade, saying their three-point demands remain unfulfilled.
According to the joint statement, emergency vehicles, including fire service vehicles, ambulances and hearse vans, will be exempt from the blockade. Vehicles carrying emergency medicine supplies and newspapers, as well as those used by journalists for news gathering, will also be allowed to pass.

item.title: Three Bangladeshis who fled Myanmar scam compound to return home Thursday
item.description:
Three Bangladeshis who fled a scam compound in Myanmar and took refuge in Thailand are scheduled to return home on Thursday.
They are expected to arrive in Dhaka at 4:20pm on US-Bangla Airlines flight BS-218, according to the scheduled itinerary.
The returnees are Md Saidur Rahman, Robiul and Md Sohel Rana.
Anirban Survivor Voice Foundation took the initiative to repatriate them following complaints from the victims and their families. On August 24, the organisation applied to the Wage Earners’ Welfare Board under the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment, seeking assistance in bringing them home.
In response, the board’s Director Md Saidur Rahman issued a letter instructing the first secretary (labour) at the Bangladesh Embassy in Bangkok to take the necessary steps.
The letter called for measures to secure the release and repatriation of eight Bangladeshis staying at a safe house under the referral mechanism of Thailand’s Mae Sot Immigration Office.
Of the eight, three are scheduled to return home on Thursday, while legal procedures are underway to repatriate the remaining five.

item.title: Toulouse v Troyes Ligue 1 game postponed as France gripped by unrest
item.description:
The Ligue 1 match between Toulouse and Troyes this weekend has has pushed back a day at the request of local authorities struggling to contain unrest in France, the French league (LFP) announced on Wednesday.
The match which had been due to take place in Toulouse in southwest France at 1715 local time (1515 GMT) on Saturday will now kick off on Sunday at the same time.
"Although not considered high-risk, organising an event with such a large turnout requires the deployment of internal security forces and municipal police personnel," the Haute-Garonne prefecture, which manages public services and security in the region, said.
A second sporting event is also scheduled in Toulouse on Saturday with the city's rugby club set to host Perpignan in a Top 14 rugby match.
On Tuesday, the Ligue 2 match between Montpellier and Paris-based Red Star originally scheduled for Saturday was moved to Monday.
Some of the worst urban violence to hit France in years erupted last Saturday on the fringe of nationwide protests over the rising cost of living.
Since then, authorities have ordered partial curfews in parts of Paris and other cities, including Toulouse, to prevent further violence.
There was tight security at the Parc des Princes in Paris on Tuesday for Paris Saint-Germain's victory against Barcelona in the Champions League.
PSG will host Lyon at the same venue in a Ligue 1 match on Sunday evening.

item.title: Ronaldo let United down says Ten Hag
item.description:
Former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag has accused Cristiano Ronaldo of letting the team down during his time in charge.
Portugal star Ronaldo was in his second spell at United when Ten Hag was hired in 2022.
Ten Hag's relationship with Ronaldo quickly became tense and the striker refused to come on as a substitute in a win over Tottenham in the October 2022.
Ronaldo was dropped for a subsequent match against Chelsea, prompting him to give an explosive television interview in which he said he felt betrayed by United and did not respect Ten Hag.
The former Real Madrid forward's contract at United was mutually terminated the following month.
"He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him," Ten Hag said in an interview with The Athletic.
"Obviously, he's one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in."
Ten Hag said Ronaldo pulled out of training sessions and did not complete the full run that players were set after they were beaten 4-0 by Brentford early in his reign.
"I confronted him with this. Many times I say, 'Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can't bring yourself in the box, you can't score'. He was not capable to do this," Ten Hag said.
"It's the wrong idea to put this to me that I expected him to do the pressing, that he's exhausted. But he couldn't.
"He ran neither in possession nor out of possession. The reason was because he didn't prepare himself."
Ten Hag also claimed promises made by United's owners went unfulfilled before he was sacked in 2024, shortly after signing a new contract.
Although United won the FA Cup just months earlier with a surprise final victory against Manchester City, Ten Hag was axed with the team languishing in 14th place in the Premier League.
The Dutchman blamed the United hierarchy of some of his problems, saying he was left humiliated when Scotland midfielder Scott McTominay was sold to Napoli without his consent.
Ten Hag also said he wanted to sign Harry Kane, Declan Rice and Frenkie de Jong during his spell at United.
"They promised me loyalty, they promised me backing, they promised communication, that we get aligned. We spoke about the issues. But the promises, they didn't keep," he said.
"I said, 'No selling Scott McTominay'. And in the end they sold him. I got, of course, very embarrassed and disappointed."

item.title: BCB reshapes HP prog with focus on int'l readiness
item.description:
The Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) has revamped its High Performance (HP) programme with a renewed focus on preparing cricketers for the demands of international cricket.
The programme would address longstanding concerns over consistency, injury management and the transition from age-group to senior-level cricket.
Traditionally, the HP programme has served as a key component of Bangladesh's cricket development pathway by identifying and nurturing promising talents for the national team.
However, an extensive review of the programme has prompted the board to rethink its approach in a bid to help players maintain consistent performances and regain form after setbacks.
One of the major concerns identified by the HP management is the difficulty players face in sustaining their performance at the international level. Cricketers who fall out of the national setup because of poor form, injuries or other reasons often struggle to regain the rhythm required to compete at the highest level.
The revamped programme will seek to address these challenges by providing elite-level players with a structured environment in which they can continue developing their skills, work on weaknesses and prepare for a return to international cricket.
The initiative will primarily target elite cricketers who are knocking at the door of national team or have previously represented Bangladesh. Current national players will also be part of the programme when they are not engaged in international commitments.
They will return to the HP setup after completing their national duties to continue refining their skills.
"The main objective is to keep them in cricket all the year round so that they make them ready for international-level cricket always," BCB assistant general manager Rabeed Imam told BSS.
"After playing a series, the analyst, coaches and other staff analyse the performance of the players and identify what they did well and what they did wrong. The HP programme will give them an opportunity to work on their problems after a particular series," he added.
The BCB is planning to bolster the programme's coaching structure in phases, appointing specialists and support staff to meet the needs of its elite players.
National team senior assistant coach Mohammad Salahuddin has already been appointed head coach, while Sohel Islam serves as senior HP coach. Former Bangladesh left-arm spinner Abdur Razzak has also joined the coaching staff, with Corey Collymore appointed as pace-bowling coach.
Bangladesh introduced the HP programme in 2004 under the BCB's Game Development Committee, then headed by Arafat Rahman Koko. Richard McInnes was appointed head coach and played a significant role in identifying and developing talents such as Tamim Iqbal, Mushfiqur Rahim and Mahmudullah Riyad, who went on to serve Bangladesh cricket for nearly two decades.
Since its inception, the HP programme has helped produce several cricketers who have contributed to the growth of the national team. However, recurring concerns about consistency and the challenges of moving from potential to sustained international performance have prompted the board to reassess its development model.
Under the revised structure, the BCB also intends to address one of Bangladesh cricket's longstanding challenges: bridging the gap between age-group cricket and the senior national team.
More often it was seen the players had played well in age level but lost the way when he was introduced into the national team.
At the same time, despite doing well in domestic circuit, the player often finds it tough to thrive in International cricket.
Rabeed said, under the revamped HP programme, there will be plan to address those issues.
"The HP programme will also focus on to keep the players in track, so that they don't find International cricket tougher one."
The programme's activities in 2026 have included a multi-format series against Zimbabwe A, an overseas tour by the Bangladesh Emerging Team to South Africa and participation in the Top End T20 tournament in Australia.
These assignments are intended to provide emerging players with valuable competitive experience against unfamiliar opposition and in different playing conditions.
The BCB has also moved to establish a dedicated Women's HP unit, signalling an expansion of its high-performance development pathway.
The BCB is also exploring opportunities to arrange more bilateral series for its HP players.
"At this moment, we have been in discussion with several countries to arrange bilateral series for HP. We'll sort it out very soon and prepare a calendar for HP," Rabeed said.
The programme is expected to evolve gradually beyond its existing framework into a comprehensive cricket academy, offering players a more integrated development environment.
Injury management and rehabilitation will receive particular attention under the new structure, with fast bowlers identified as a group requiring more effective support because of the physical demands of their role.
Injuries have frequently interrupted the development of Bangladesh's fast bowlers, limiting their availability for domestic and international cricket.
"A stronger rehabilitation framework could help reduce these disruptions by integrating medical assessments, physiotherapy, strength and conditioning, workload monitoring and carefully managed returns to bowling," Rabeed added.

item.title: Infantino to take FIFA re-election campaign to Japan to court Asian soccer federations
item.description:
Gianni Infantino is set to take his FIFA presidential re-election campaign to Japan this week, where he is scheduled to meet leaders of the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) on Wednesday.
The meeting comes after Infantino apologised last week in Zurich, Switzerland, to FIFA's 37-member ruling council, which he chairs, for "mistakes" in putting together a now-abandoned $4.2 billion plan to sell off World Cup commercial rights.
The council is FIFA's main decision-making body, comprising officials from across the world.
The planned meeting with Asian soccer leaders will take place at a five-star hotel in Tokyo, with media access largely restricted.
Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, the AFC president, initially opposed Infantino and his proposal to establish a subsidiary to run the World Cup. However, he may have moved closer to the FIFA president, according to a report by The Athletic.
Infantino has offered his critics an open and independent review of FIFA's decision-making process.
Infantino seeks support ahead of election
An Associated Press tally suggests Infantino is nearing the simple majority of votes from FIFA's 211 member federations needed to secure re-election in March for a fourth term. Some decisive votes could come from Asia.
The AFC had joined criticism of Infantino following the proposed World Cup commercial rights sell-off, but its members appear divided over his leadership. Qatar, host of the 2022 World Cup, has expressed support for Infantino, while Jordan has declared its opposition.
The FIFA Council is scheduled to hold its next meeting on Dec 16 in Doha, Qatar.
According to the AP tally, 87 of FIFA's 211 member federations have indicated support for Infantino, either through individual comments or by endorsing statements of backing issued by their regional confederations. Europe accounts for the largest bloc of opposition.
FIFA's election rules
No incumbent FIFA president has lost an election since 1974. The deadline for candidates to submit nominations to challenge Infantino is Nov 18.
Under FIFA rules, candidates must have "played an active role in association football (e.g. as a player or an official within FIFA, a confederation or an association, etc.) for two of the last five years before being proposed."
They must also secure declarations of support from at least five of FIFA's 211 member federations.
"FIFA is a massive patronage network," Jules Boykoff, a political scientist at Pacific University and a former professional soccer player, told the Associated Press.
"It brings in billions from the men's World Cup and distributes it to football associations around the world in exchange for loyalty," he said.
"The funds that FIFA distributes to soccer bodies around the world are meant to develop soccer, but there's scant oversight," Boykoff added. "To say FIFA is in need of structural overhaul it to make an enormous understatement."

item.title: The making of Bangladesh’s architectural excellence
item.description:
The Royal Institute of British Architects’ (RIBA) prestigious International Prize has been awarded to Karupannya’s Green Field factory in Rangpur.
Designed by the soft-spoken and unassuming architect Bayezid Khondker and his practice, Nakhsabid Architects, this is yet another architectural feather in our cap. And this is not the first time a building from Bangladesh has won the award.
Friendship Hospital in Satkhira, designed by architect Kashef Chowdhury, won the prize in 2021.
Since the prize’s inception in 2015, there have been five winners, two of them from Bangladesh.
The Karupannya factory was selected from four shortlisted projects, two of which were from Bangladesh, the other being the BRAC University campus in Dhaka, designed by WOHA, an architectural practice based in Singapore.
The shortlist was drawn from 34 projects recognised in the RIBA International Awards for Excellence 2026.
Louis Kahn lecturing at BUET in the 1960’s. Photo: Collected
The list included another project from Bangladesh: the Zebun Nessa Mosque, designed by Saiqa Iqbal Meghna of the practice Morphogenesis.
Bangladeshi architects have won numerous notable international awards for their work.
These include the prestigious Aga Khan Award for Architecture.
Kashef Chowdhury and Marina Tabassum won the award separately in 2016, followed by Saiful Haque in 2019, and Khondaker Hasibul Kabir and Suhailey Farzana, Rizvi Hassan, Khwaja Fathmi and Saad Ben Mostafa in 2022.
Marina Tabassum won again in 2025, setting a record by becoming a two-time recipient of the award.
Other projects in Bangladesh that have received this award include the Grameen Bank Housing Project and the Bangladesh National Parliament building, designed by Louis I Kahn.
Bangladesh has the second-highest number of projects to have won this award, after Iran. Another recipient was Bangladeshi structural engineer FR Khan for his design of the Hajj Terminal at Jeddah Airport.
Bangladeshi architects have also received countless international awards and recognitions over the years.
These include awards from the Commonwealth Association of Architects (CAA), the JK Cement Awards, the International Union of Architects (UIA), and ARCASIA, among others. Listing all the awards and their recipients would leave little room to discuss the actual subject of this article.
Given that Bangladesh is a small country with about 5,000 registered architects, compared with approximately 150,000 in India, 6,000 in Pakistan, 130,000 in the United States and 28,000 in the United Kingdom, it can confidently be said that we have performed better than our neighbours, including India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Malaysia.
The Architecture building at BUET. Photo: Collected
Why is this so? Is there something we have that others do not? Is it genetic? Is it training and education? Or is it passion? It is difficult to pinpoint any single reason or even draw up a definitive list of reasons.
If one were to examine the background that has produced good architects in Bangladesh, several possible explanations might emerge. There is no empirical evidence, data or research to support these explanations. They are simply observations about the culture of architecture in the country.
We have Muzharul Islam, the pioneering modern architect of the country and the region, and examples of his world-class architectural projects, built from shortly after Partition through to the 1980s. In him, we also have an architect who set an example not only through outstanding buildings but also through high ethical standards and devotion to the profession, not to mention his eloquent, sophisticated and articulate personality.
Bangladeshi architects, almost without exception, recognise him as a ‘guru’ and look to his high standards as an example to follow. His creations, including the Charukala Institute, the Dhaka University Library, the NIPA building and the two universities, continue to be landmarks and sources of inspiration. For students, visiting some of his buildings is almost like a pilgrimage.
Then there is the National Parliament building complex, designed by Louis I Kahn. The Parliament building itself is recognised as one of the hundred most influential buildings of the last century.
Muzharul Islam was instrumental in bringing Kahn, an internationally recognised master architect, to this country. Islam believed that our country should have an exemplary work by a renowned architect of the time, just as India had Le Corbusier, and convinced the government to engage Kahn. This was Islam’s gift to the younger generation of architects. Architects and students continue to study this remarkable example and draw inspiration from it.
In the 1960s, quite a few internationally renowned architects worked here. Paul Rudolph designed several buildings at Mymensingh Agricultural University. Constantin Doxiadis designed the Teacher-Student Centre (TSC) at Dhaka University, the Home Economics College and the BARD complex in Cumilla, among others. Muzharul Islam and Stanley Tigerman jointly designed five polytechnic institutes.
There were others, such as Robert Bouighey, Richard Vrooman and Daniel Dunham, who were less widely known but designed buildings that inspired our architects. These included Kamalapur Railway Station, halls of residence at BUET and Dhaka University, the Faculty of Architecture and Planning at BUET, and buildings at Rajshahi University, among others. These buildings are excellent examples of tropical modernism and provide valuable lessons for architects.
Friendship Hospital, Satkhira. Photo: Courtesy of Kashef Chowdhury
The Department of Architecture at the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET), then known as the East Pakistan University of Engineering and Technology, introduced an undergraduate program in architecture in 1962.
It was initially established by a group of American teachers from Texas A&M University. They included Richard Vrooman, who was the first dean and the architect of the faculty building. The building is still in use and remains cherished by students and alumni alike. Other teachers included Daniel Dunham and Walden, among others.
They taught a small group of students for several years until Bangladeshi teachers who had been sent abroad returned to take over around 1967–68.
From the very beginning, the department developed a ‘culture’ in which architecture was treated with the utmost seriousness as a profession. There was an almost sacred devotion to the subject, something approaching religious conviction. Students and teachers alike were deeply committed.
The building itself helped foster this culture, with its spacious corridors, large studios and an open ground floor supported by columns, now known as the ‘plinth’. It became a place for serious discussions and arguments.
I have not encountered this kind of passion in any other school, although I have taught at several institutions abroad and visited many others.
Let me cite a small incident that exemplifies this almost religious devotion.
A younger colleague, who was also a former student, and I were teaching architectural graphics to freshmen. My colleague was explaining how to set up their drawing sheets on the table.
He said, “First, go and wash your hands carefully with soap and dry them.”
When the students had done so and returned to class, he explained how the drawing sheet had to be aligned with the parallel bar and fixed to the table with tape, and how pencils needed to be sharpened—preferably by hand with a blade rather than a sharpener, then further sharpened using grade 0 sandpaper and dipped into Styrofoam to remove graphite granules.
Once that was done, he said, “Now go and wash your hands again.”
When they returned, he told them, “Now approach your work as if you are performing ‘ebadad’, meaning prayer.”
The entire ritual of washing one’s hands twice before approaching the task with the devotion of prayer had to be followed. Such was the culture.
The carefully designed admission process ensured that only students with a genuine interest in architecture were admitted.
There was a separate admission test for architecture, with 80% of the questions assessing creative and drawing skills and the remaining 20% covering mathematics. The mathematics questions were exceptionally difficult, going beyond what students had learned at the HSC level, and candidates did not have to pass that section separately to qualify.
I believe this was quite deliberate, ensuring that students could not gain admission solely on the strength of their mathematical knowledge.
The result was that students who genuinely wanted to study architecture and possessed drawing and artistic skills were admitted, although the competition was intense. The studios appeared to have a more artistic than technical orientation.
Unfortunately, that admission system was discontinued in 1999, and there is now a common admission test for the whole of BUET. Eight architecture faculty members resigned in protest and left.
Now, this department was housed within a technical university where the majority of programs were in engineering. In technically oriented universities around the world, architecture programs tend to have a technical inclination. But at BUET, architecture was artistic.
Moreover, the faculty building occupied its own separate space, away from engineering.
Students and faculty members from other disciplines often regarded architecture as a less serious subject than their own. Architecture was ridiculed, and there were taunts about architecture students doing little more than drawing trees and similar things.
The subject was even referred to as “yarki-tecture”, with yarki being the Bangla word for joke or banter.
This no longer happens. Bangladeshi architects have proved themselves and have received more international accolades than members of any other profession in the country.
Such was the devotion to and seriousness about architecture.
Meanwhile, the country’s economy began to grow, creating opportunities for architects to showcase their work. Architecture has become a popular profession, and there are now more than 30 architecture programs across the country.
There may be other reasons why Bangladesh produces such good architects, but I cannot say with certainty what they are.
Today, apart from the architects who have already won awards, there is an emerging generation of talented young architects producing excellent work.
This tradition of good architecture will continue.
The author is the Dean of the School of Architecture and Design at Brac University and the founder of its architecture program. He is a graduate of BUET and has also taught there.

item.title: Yemen’s Houthis say targeted Saudi position in Aden
item.description:
Yemen’s Houthis said they attacked a Saudi position in the city of Aden on Wednesday, with smoke seen rising near the airport, in the third attack in a week on the seat of power of Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government.
“Our armed forces were able to target the Saudi enemy’s operations room in the Badr camp in Aden with a ballistic missile,” Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement.
A police official in Aden earlier told AFP there had been a blast “caused by a Houthi missile,” speaking on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
Two other security sources in the city told AFP the attack targeted a site near the airport that belonged to forces from the Saudi-led military coalition which has been battling the Houthis.
The Houthis later also targeted a military base at an airport in the southern city of Al Mukalla, two military officials told AFP.
“The Houthis used missiles and drones to target a military base housing forces from the Saudi-led coalition at Al Rayyan airport,” said one of the officials, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Saree said the group had targeted “military equipment transported by the Saudi enemy via military cargo planes to Al Rayyan airport.”
Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognized Yemeni government have come under sustained attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, shifting the focus of the wider Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
On Friday, two missiles landed within the perimeter of the airport in Aden, with the Houthis claiming the attack.
A day earlier, the Houthis launched a deadly missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden, hitting command centers located inside the Al-Maashiq presidential compound, which is used by government forces and the Saudi-led coalition.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen’s capital Sanaa in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing government-held territory in Yemen along the Red Sea coastline in a lightning campaign.
In response, the Saudi air force has been regularly targeting the Houthis in support of the Yemeni government.

item.title: Three of a family critically burned in Tongi gas cylinder explosion
item.description:
Three members of the same family, including a woman and a teenage girl, suffered severe burn injuries in a gas cylinder explosion in Tongi, Gazipur, on Wednesday morning.
The victims were admitted to the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery in Dhaka, where their conditions were described as critical.
The incident occurred around 6am in an area near Cherag Ali Market under Tongi West police station.
One of the victims, Lalchan, 60, suffered burns to 95% of his body and is receiving treatment in the hospital's emergency department.
Tanisha, 16, a student, sustained burns to 86% of her body and has been admitted to the Female High Dependency Unit (FHDU). Nasima, 50, suffered burns to 85% of her body and is also receiving treatment in the emergency department.
Sultan Mahmud Sikdar, resident surgeon at the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery, said the victims' conditions were critical due to the extensive burns. Hospital staff were making every effort to save them.
Preliminary assessments suggest that the explosion occurred when accumulated gas from a leaking cylinder ignited.

item.title: Human trafficking on the rise along Teknaf coast
item.description:
Enamul Haque Kayes, a physically disabled man from Teknaf, was the sole breadwinner for his family. He worked at a Bonoful shop in Hnila until he went missing about 10 days ago. After searching for him in vain, his family learned that he was among 76 people rescued by the Bangladesh Navy off Saint Martin’s Island.
His family alleges that Kayes was abducted and sold to traffickers who attempted to smuggle him to Malaysia by sea.
His case highlights growing concerns along the Teknaf coast, where trafficking networks are reportedly using abduction, confinement and ransom demands to force victims into dangerous sea journeys.
As calmer seas create favourable conditions for maritime crossings, trafficking networks have become active again. Over the past week, law enforcement agencies have rescued more than 150 people, including Rohingya refugees, and arrested at least 15 suspected brokers.
Kayes’s father, Ahmudul Rahman, said his son was the family’s sole breadwinner.
“My son has a disability, but he was the only person supporting our family financially. We searched everywhere but could not find him. Later, I learnt that he was among those rescued by the Navy,” he said.
Ayat Ullah, a ninth-grade student at Teknaf Government Technical School and College, was also among those rescued. He said his abductors took him to a hill near the Mochoni Rohingya camp, where he was held captive with others.
His captors initially sold him to a broker for Tk30,000. The broker then sold him to another person for Tk1 lakh, he said.
After nearly a month in captivity, Ayat and the others were taken to Kachhapia in Baharchhara and put aboard a trawler off Marine Drive.
“After three days at sea, the boat broke down and water began entering it. We thought we might never make it back alive. Later, the Navy rescued us,” he said.
In another incident, armed men abducted Mostak Ahmed from Hnila union at gunpoint and demanded Tk10 lakh from his family. He was released three days later after his family paid Tk5 lakh following negotiations.
Mohammad Saber, 32, from Kochubania in Sabrang union, said his abductors held and tortured him for three days to force his family to pay a ransom. He was later trafficked to Malaysia via Myanmar and Thailand.
Saber returned to Bangladesh on October 9, 2024, after nearly four years abroad. Injuries sustained during his captivity left lasting damage to his head and eyes, preventing him from working normally.
In recent operations, police rescued 16 people, including Rohingya refugees, from Kachhapia. Border Guard Bangladesh and police also dismantled 20 suspected trafficking hideouts in the hills of Rajarchhara, rescuing 16 people reportedly abducted for trafficking and arresting a suspected broker. The SRB separately rescued five people from Kachhapia.
A M Faruk, assistant director (law and media) of SRB-15, said operations were underway to identify and arrest those involved. He called for greater public awareness and cooperation to combat human trafficking.
Between 2016 and 2025, a total of 3,534 people travelling towards Malaysia were rescued off the Cox’s Bazar coast, most of them Rohingya refugees. A total of 120 cases were filed with Ukhiya and Teknaf police stations over such incidents.
Meanwhile, 330 people were reportedly abducted in Teknaf over the past three years. Locals alleged that victims unable to pay ransom were often sold to trafficking networks.
The dangers extend far beyond captivity. In a joint statement, the UN refugee agency and the International Organization for Migration said more than 500 people were feared dead after two boats carrying Rohingya refugees sank off Myanmar’s Rakhine State in June. The agencies also reported that around 300 Rohingya refugees and Bangladeshis had died or gone missing this year while attempting dangerous sea journeys.
Belal Mia, a farmer from Teknaf Sadar, was among those missing after a trawler sank in the Andaman Sea. His pregnant wife, Ayesha Begum, said brokers had forcibly put her husband aboard a boat. She has received no news of him for nearly three months.
More than 600 human trafficking cases were filed in Cox’s Bazar between 2012 and 2026, according to district police and the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers’ Association. Around 480 remain pending, including more than 300 in Ukhiya and Teknaf.
Biswajit Bhowmik, a lawyer with the association, said Cox’s Bazar lacked a dedicated tribunal for human trafficking and migrant smuggling cases, contributing to lengthy trials.
Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC’s migration programme, said traffickers were increasingly resorting to abduction alongside deception and false promises of marriage or employment.
Cox’s Bazar Additional Superintendent of Police Md Ahidur Rahman said abduction and trafficking were closely linked, with some victims being trafficked when their captors failed to obtain ransom payments. He said law enforcement agencies were continuing raids and intelligence operations to bring those responsible to justice.

item.title: President calls for nat'l committee to ensure equal rights for all
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Wednesday called for the formation of a national committee to ensure equal civic rights and facilities for people of all religions in Bangladesh.
“Religion is personal, but the state belongs to all. Everyone has the right to security and justice,” he said, stressing that Hindus, Muslims, Buddhists and Christians are all citizens of the country and are entitled to equal rights, dignity and religious freedom under the Constitution.
The President made the remarks while exchanging greetings with members of the Hindu community at Bangabhaban on the occasion of Sharadiya Durga Puja and Bijoya Dashami 2026. His wife Rahat Ara Begum was present.
Emphasising the importance of communal harmony, Mirza Fakhrul said while wars, violence and communal conflicts are taking place in different parts of the world, people of all religions in Bangladesh are celebrating their respective festivals peacefully.
“This harmony is our strength and our very existence. We must preserve it at all costs,” he said.
The President warned that attempts are sometimes made to create divisions through rumours, misinformation and religious extremism, urging a firm and uncompromising stance against such efforts.
He urged the younger generation, in particular, to speak out in favour of truth, justice and humanity.
“The country belongs to all of us, and we must build it together. No evil force should be allowed to undermine national unity and progress by creating divisions,” Mirza Fakhrul said.
He called for building a safe, democratic, humane and welfare-oriented Bangladesh founded on mutual respect, equality and social justice.
Describing Bangladesh as a country of communal harmony, the President said people of different faiths have lived together on this land for thousands of years in an atmosphere of mutual respect and brotherhood.
He also noted that the participation of people from all religious communities in the War of Liberation, democratic struggles and movements against injustice laid the foundation for national unity.
Greeting members of the Hindu community on Bijoya Dashami, Mirza Fakhrul said he was delighted to welcome them to Bangabhaban for the festive occasion.
He said the underlying message of the festival is the destruction of evil and the triumph of truth, beauty and welfare.
“No citizen should face discrimination or persecution because of their religion, ethnicity or community identity,” the President said.
He said law enforcement agencies and the administration have been directed to remain highly vigilant to ensure that people of all faiths can practise their religions in a safe and joyful environment.
Earlier, when the President arrived at the Credential Hall of Bangabhaban, leaders of the Hindu Religious Welfare Trust, Bangladesh Hindu-Buddhist-Christian Welfare Front, Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad and the Mahanagar Sarbojanin Puja Committee greeted him with flowers.
Mirza Fakhrul and his wife exchanged greetings with visitors and guests who attended the event.
Religious Affairs Minister Kazi Shah Mofazzal Houssain Kaikobad, State Minister Mohammad Shamim Kaiser, Prime Minister's Special Assistant Bijon Kanti Sarkar and senior officials of the President's Office were also present.

item.title: Hospital vandalized in Savar over child's death during surgery
item.description:
An 11-year-old boy died after undergoing surgery at Abbas Specialized Hospital in Savar on Wednesday, prompting his relatives to vandalize the facility.
The child, Abraham, was undergoing surgery for nasal polyps and tonsil problems at the hospital in Ulail, Savar municipality, when the incident occurred. His family alleged that medical negligence led to his death.
Abraham was the son of Abdul Alim, an expatriate worker from the Singair area of Manikganj.
Following the incident, the accused physician, Dr Md Sumon Hossain, and other doctors, nurses and officials left the hospital. They could not be reached for comment. The mobile phone of hospital owner Dr Md Abbas Uddin was also found switched off.
Abraham’s mother, Kona Akter, said her son had been suffering from nasal polyps and tonsil problems. She took him to Dr Sumon at Abbas Specialized Hospital a few days ago, when the physician advised surgery and prescribed an electrocardiogram (ECG) and echocardiogram (echo) as preoperative tests.
She said an ECG was performed at the hospital on Tuesday, but the echo could not be done because the doctor was unavailable. When she told Dr Sumon that she would have the echo done elsewhere, he reportedly said the ECG results were satisfactory and the echo was unnecessary.
Following the doctor’s advice, Kona took her son to the hospital at around 11:30am on Wednesday, and he was taken to the operating theatre.
About an hour and a half later, doctors and nurses began rushing around outside the operating theatre and informed her that her son had developed complications and needed intensive care, she said.
On their advice, she took him to Enam Medical College Hospital in Savar at around 2pm, where doctors declared him dead.
“My son died because of wrong treatment. I want justice for what happened,” Kona said, alleging medical negligence.
Dr Abdul Ahad, a medical officer at the intensive care unit of Enam Medical College Hospital, confirmed the child’s death.
“When the child was brought to us, there were no signs of a heartbeat or other signs of life. After examining him and confirming his death, we informed his family,” he said.
Asked about the possible cause of death, Dr Ahad said he had heard that the child’s condition deteriorated after he was administered anaesthesia at the other hospital.
A visit to Abbas Specialized Hospital after the incident found several patients still admitted, but no doctors or nurses were present, leaving those receiving treatment in a difficult situation.
One patient, Sirajul Islam, said he had been unable to find any doctor or nurse since the vandalism in the afternoon.
“I have also undergone surgery. I do not know what to do in this situation,” he said.
A security guard stationed outside the hospital, who declined to be named, said the doctors, nurses and other staff had left after the incident. Most patients had also departed, with only two or three remaining, he added.
Attempts to contact hospital owner Dr Abbas Uddin and Dr Sumon for comment were unsuccessful, as both of their mobile phones were switched off.
Savar Upazila Health and Family Planning Officer Dr Md Fazle Bari said he had learned that a child had died in the hospital’s operating theatre.
“However, no one has filed a complaint with us. We will take action if a complaint is lodged,” he said.
Savar Model police station Sub-Inspector Fazr Ali said police found no incision marks on the child’s body during the inquest. However, there were signs of bleeding from his nose and mouth.
He said police had heard that the child died after being administered anaesthetic medication. The child’s relatives subsequently vandalized the hospital, he added.

item.title: Document: Two Bangladeshis executed in Saudi Arabia detained since Aug 2023
item.description:
The two Bangladeshi nationals, who were recently executed in Saudi Arabia, had been detained in the country since August 2023 on separate charges, according to a confidential document from the Labour Welfare Wing of the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah. The two were identified as Nazrul Islam Abdul Bashir and Sweety Akter.
The document, sent to the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment on October 18, said there was no previous record of any Bangladeshi national being executed in Saudi Arabia on charges related to information technology offences or adultery.
Besides, the Saudi authorities did not inform the Bangladesh Embassy or the consulate before the executions, nor did they formally notify them afterwards about the executions, it said.
The information about the execution emerged from Saudi media reports citing a statement issued by the Saudi Ministry of Interior on October 14.
According to the Saudi ministry’s statement, as reported in local media, the executions took place in the Makkah region. They were accused of committing “indecent acts” inside a mosque in the holy city of Makkah.
The consulate said Saudi authorities did not provide detailed information about the cases.
The document said the consulate had earlier sought information from the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Bangladeshi nationals detained for various offences in prisons across western Saudi Arabia.
A list received on September 30 included the names of Nazrul and Sweety but did not specify their sentences. Both were reportedly employed as cleaners at an establishment called Al-Majal.
According to the list, Nazrul was detained on August 1, 2023, on charges related to information technology offences, while Sweety was detained on August 2 on an “adultery charge”.
Nazrul had been held at the Jeddah Correctional Facility, while Sweety was held at the Jeddah Women’s Prison.
The consulate said the list contained no information about the sentences handed down to either of them.
It also noted that videos of unrelated or past incidents were being circulated on social media in connection with the executions. According to the document, 306 Bangladeshi nationals were being held in prisons across western Saudi Arabia in connection with various morality-related cases. Of them, 147 were sentenced to prison terms ranging from one month to 15 years.
The consulate said it had received no requests for legal assistance or other communication from the families of the two executed individuals.
Saudi authorities had also not informed the consulate of their sentences or executions.
The consulate has sent a diplomatic note to the Makkah branch of the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs seeking copies of the verdicts and detailed information about the cases.
A comprehensive report will be submitted after the documents are received, according to the document.
