item.title: Durga Puja ends with immersion of idols
item.description:
Durga Puja, the biggest religious festival of the Hindu community, ended in Bangladesh on Wednesday with the immersion of idols of Goddess Durga and her children in water bodies across the country.
According to Hindu belief, Durga has returned to her husband's abode at Kailash in Devaloy through the immersion.
In the capital, thousands of people thronged the Buriganga River to observe the final phase of the festival -- immersion of the goddess.
The Sharadiya Durga Puja, the main religious festival of Hindus, concluded on Wednesday with the immersion of idols. On the occasion of Bijoya Dashami, devotees brought idols of Goddess Durga from various puja mandaps across the capital to Basila Launch Ghat. They immersed the idols there following traditional rituals. Photo: Abir Ahmmed Shupto/Dhaka Tribune
Hindu devotees from different parts of the city came to the ghat in trucks carrying idols while singing hymns to Durga with the sounds of musical instruments such as "Shankha", "Khol", "Dhak".
Devotees were seen bidding farewell to the mother deity and her children - Lakshmi, Saraswati, Kartik and Ganesh - through the immersion of their idols, wishing Durga's return next year.
As part of the main rituals of Dashami Puja celebrations, female devotees offered vermilion at the feet of Durga at mandaps and temples across the city.
Hindu devotees, particularly women, celebrated Bijoya Dashami with sindur khela, dance and music at different Durga Puja mandaps across the capital.
The Sharadiya Durga Puja, the main religious festival of Hindus, concluded on Wednesday with the immersion of idols. On the occasion of Bijoya Dashami, devotees brought idols of Goddess Durga from various puja mandaps across the capital to Basila Launch Ghat. They immersed the idols there following traditional rituals. Photo: Abir Ahmmed Shupto/Dhaka Tribune
Women then smeared sindur on one another’s foreheads and cheeks, sharing joy and exchanging greetings amid the festive atmosphere.
The mandaps came alive with dancing and music to the rhythmic beats of traditional drums as devotees celebrated the final day of the Sharadiya Durga Puja.
At the poignant and sorrowful moment of Bijoya, the idol of Goddess Durga was brought out of the Dhakeshwari National Temple.
After offering a final glimpse of their beloved goddess, devotees set off with the idol for immersion.
Following six days of worship, celebrations and prayers, emotions and sadness were reflected on the faces of devotees as they bid farewell to Durga.
The six-day festival started on October 16 with the incarnation of Goddess Durga. This year, Maha Saptami was celebrated for days.
Durga Puja, the annual Hindu festival also known as Sharadiya (autumnal) Durga Utsab, is the worship of "Shakti", the divine force, embodied in Goddess Durga.
It symbolises the battle between good and evil, where the dark forces eventually succumb to the divine.
This year, Durga Puja was celebrated at 33,165 mandaps across the country.

item.description:
Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Md Asaduzzaman on Wednesday urged teachers to take timely and well-planned decisions to keep the present generation away from drugs and guide them towards the right path.
"It is becoming increasingly difficult for teachers to manage the current generation, while students' inclination towards drugs is growing. To address the situation, students must be given fresh consideration and effective initiatives suited to their needs should be taken," he said.
The minister made the remarks while addressing a views-exchange meeting with local teachers and journalists as the chief guest at the Shailkupa Upazila BNP office in the district.
He said it is essential to keep students away from drugs and ensure a proper educational environment.
"To this end, teachers must play their roles responsibly and take planned steps considering the needs and realities of the current generation," said Asaduzzaman.
Expressing a firm stance against irregularities in recruitment and management at educational institutions, he said no one would be spared if financial transactions take place in recruitment at any institution.
The minister also said it is unacceptable for a chairman of a school management committee to behave rudely towards the head teacher.
He said it would also be intolerable if teachers disrupt the educational environment for students or became involved in wrongdoing. Everyone concerned should behave responsibly to maintain a healthy environment at educational institutions, he added.
Emphasising the responsibility of political leadership in preventing corruption, Asaduzzaman said political leaders and party activists must first make themselves corruption-free to stop corruption.
Those who speak about ending corruption must reflect that commitment in their own conduct; otherwise, efforts to prevent corruption would fail, he added.
Shailkupa Upazila BNP President Abul Hossain, General Secretary Humayun Babar Firoz, teachers from private schools, colleges and madrasas in the upazila, and journalists from various print and electronic media attended the views-exchange meeting.

item.title: Khulna’s Super Jute Mill struggles under mounting debt
item.description:
Super Jute Mill, once one of Bangladesh’s leading private-sector exporters of jute products, is now struggling under mounting debt, raising fears of bankruptcy. The mill, which once earned Tk20-30 lakh a day and exported products to 24 countries, has seen its fortunes reverse amid a prolonged financing crisis.
Superex Leather, another company owned by the same entrepreneur, is also facing a financial crisis.
Entrepreneur M Firoz Ahmed Bhuiyan has blamed the downturn on a lack of bank financing, while Islami Bank Bangladesh PLC says the company has failed to present a specific loan repayment plan and repay instalments.
Established in 2006 at Alka village of Phultala upazila with an investment of around Tk250 crore, Super Jute Mill employed nearly 5,000 people and became a leading private-sector exporter. Its products gained demand in 24 countries, and the company received state awards three times for its contribution to exports. Management sources said its daily profit once reached Tk30 lakh, while foreign buyers often paid in advance.
Following the mill’s success, Islami Bank reportedly assured Bhuiyan of substantial financing. In 2016, he invested around Tk700 crore to establish Superex Leather in a village of Khulna.
The factory installed advanced imported machinery, obtained Leather Working Group (LWG) certification and set up an effluent treatment plant imported from Italy at a cost of around $14 lakh. Management sources described it as one of three factories in Bangladesh recognised as green companies.
However, a shortage of working capital hampered operations. The company purchased leather worth around Tk150 crore using its own funds, but failed to secure bank financing for the chemicals and other materials needed for processing. Consequently, the price of the leather fell from Tk80 to around Tk20 per square foot.
Bhuiyan said production and business had gradually contracted after the bank stopped providing necessary working capital after 2017. He alleged that the group controlling the bank at the time sought to weaken his profitable businesses by withholding financing and eventually take them over.
He said Superex Leather was once valued at around Tk700 crore, against bank liabilities of approximately Tk600 crore. The outstanding debt has since risen to around Tk900 crore, including principal and interest.
Bhuiyan said the factories could resume production if the bank provided support, adding that they had sought around Tk200 crore in working capital.
Islami Bank’s Daulatpur branch manager Iftekhar Hossain said the company had yet to submit a specific loan repayment plan. He added that it had not taken advantage of an opportunity under a special Bangladesh Bank circular to regularise its defaulted loans by depositing 2% of the outstanding amount, complicating further lending.

item.title: What Earth’s sixth mass extinction event means for humans
item.description:
From the tiniest microbes in the human gut to giant whales in the ocean, biodiversity is the sum of all life on the planet. It’s another word for nature. And because nature is like a team, every player has a job.
When various species from trees to animals work together, they regulate weather, maintain soil health, purify water and support food production. These benefits are known as ecosystem services and they underpin human well-being.
“It is really an abstract concept, but we experience it absolutely every day,” said Rebecca Shaw, chief scientist at conservation group WWF. “And we almost never think about it when nature is functioning.”
But as biodiversity declines, Shaw and other scientists are calling on the world to really think about it. Because biodiversity is struggling as humans push ecosystems to the brink through intensive farming, burning fossil fuels and pollution from sources like plastic and chemicals.
Over the past 52 years, monitored vertebrate populations have collapsed by an average of 73%, while freshwater ecosystems are faring worse with a drop of 85%, according to WWF’s recent Living Planet report.
It tallies with other studies that show a million animal and plant species face extinction unless humanity reduces its pressure on nature.
“It is a really steep decline,” said Shaw. “What it’s telling us is that nature is in trouble, and it’s an early warning indicator that the fabric of life that we depend on for freshwater and food and for clean air is unraveling.”
Some 200 countries are gathering in Yerevan, Armenia over the next two weeks for COP17, the latest UN biodiversity summit, to advance commitments to reverse nature’s unraveling by 2030. But progress toward those targets remains insufficient, with funding and implementation among the biggest challenges.
Take wetlands as an example. Some 85% of these vital ecosystems disappeared between 1700 and 2000. One study from Canada’s University of Waterloo found that habitats like marshes and swamps in southern Ontario provide C$4.2 billion worth of water filtration services each year, removing nutrients like phosphorus and keeping drinking water sources clean.
The study found that as they disappear, water quality worsens, which massively increases the cost of treating it.
Another example is the decline in pollinators like bees and bats. More than 75% of global food crop types rely in part on animal pollination.
At the same time, soil and ecosystem degradation coupled with storms and heat waves linked to climate change are already damaging harvests. A recent UK government report stated that every critical ecosystem is on a “pathway to collapse,” warning that nature’s decline posed a grave threat to global food supply and geopolitical stability.
“The UK, like many other countries, relies on imports for much of the food and so is reliant on ecosystems around the world,” said Louise McRae, a research fellow at the Zoological Society of London, who also contributed to WWF’s Living Planet report. “This is why we need to care about global biodiversity.”
Nature also provides the basis for many modern human medicines, with some 50% coming from natural compounds.
Penicillin, the first antibiotic, is produced by a mold and is estimated to have saved over 500 million lives. Before its discovery, a person could die from a simple cut. Around 70% of cancer drugs come from natural products or synthetic compounds “inspired by nature,” according to the World Health Organization.
As biodiversity disappears, humans risk losing access to undiscovered treatments.
To return to the “nature as a team” metaphor, if a player disappears, sometimes a species with similar functions in the ecosystem can jump in as a substitute.
But not always, particularly if it’s a “keystone species.” They play a disproportionately large role in their environments, and their disappearance has significant knock-on effects.
The oyster is one such species. Wild oyster populations are facing massive declines, while 85% of their reefs have been lost worldwide. An adult oyster filters up to 50 gallons of water a day.
“No one would ever think they did anything but sit in a shell and be slimy,” said Shaw. “But you lose oysters, you can lose water filtration and clean water, you can lose the habitat for many other species that we interact with or sometimes consume.”
And, said Shaw, the humble oyster protects coastal communities from storm surges. If you lose it “you lose the coastal protection.”
The loss of a single species can also lead to more disease. One study suggests a decline in red foxes in North America is linked to the spread of Lyme disease, a tick-borne illness that also affects humans.
Extinction is a natural process. But the planet has experienced five mass extinctions, when a large proportion of species globally disappeared over a short geological period. The rate at which species are disappearing today suggests Earth is experiencing a sixth event driven largely by human activity, according to scientists.
Both McRae and Shaw called the declines extremely worrying, but said they shouldn’t provoke despair.
Though she acknowledges that the underlying global trend is moving in the wrong direction and cannot be ignored, McRae said “the statistics are there to just motivate us to action rather than to cause alarm.”
And the Living Planet report also highlights conservation successes, showing that nature can recover.
The number of green sea turtles, for example, had fallen significantly, but has now bounced back. This is thanks to a massive worldwide effort to protect nesting beaches and changes to fishing practices that reduce accidental capture.
Sea otters are another example. Prized for their fur, in the 1800s they were hunted to near extinction on the US Pacific Coast. When they disappeared, it meant sea urchins had no predators, leaving them free to decimate kelp forests.
That matters because as well as providing habitat for other species, these giant underwater groves protect coastlines from storm surges and absorb carbon, making them important for climate protection.
Following a ban on commercial hunting, sea otters have also rebounded, helping kelp forests recover.
“You can see that ripple effect that really had an obvious and a measurable impact. But critically, it can be reversed,” said McRae, adding that biodiversity loss and climate change are intertwined and exacerbate each other but have joint solutions.
“We’re learning how to turn things around at very small scales,” said Shaw. “Now the real challenge is to turn things around at very big scale so we can see it in the global indicators.”

item.title: Macron takes aim at Trump for using France riots for election gain
item.description:
President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday took an apparent swipe at counterpart Donald Trump of exploiting France’s riots for advantage in the US midterm election battle, as Paris prepared for more protests this weekend.
Macron, speaking during a visit to Qatar, implied that Trump, and possibly Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is also in election mode, made “stupid comments” on the unrest for political gain, though he did not name either leader.
“There are people who campaign at France’s expense -- leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic,” he told reporters in Doha.
Macron made his remarks as he and his government struggled to get on top of a crisis that has scarred France’s image both abroad and in financial markets, six months ahead of presidential elections to choose his successor.
France’s government has admitted it “lost control” in the frenzy of street violence that erupted last weekend, when masked youths clashed with police, looted shops and vandalized public buildings.
Trump has sought to link the “revolution” in France to “migrants, jihadists, and communists” as he campaigned for his Republican party in the United States on his anti-immigration messaging.
He also on Tuesday hailed French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who shares his ideologies, as a conservative voice, with surveys putting her as the frontrunner in France’s presidential race.
Trump’s ally Netanyahu, facing his own tough election battle, on Tuesday argued that France had been hit by an “invasion of extremist Islam.”
Several analysts have dismissed the claims that migrants were driving France’s protests.
The unrest overshadowed demonstrations held Saturday in which more than half a million people marched nationwide against the cost of living. Those rallies followed four weeks of student protests that have closed many schools across France.
Since the rioting -- the worst France has seen in years -- and ahead of further cost-of-living demonstrations this coming Saturday, Macron’s government has warned it will brook no further violence.
Authorities in Paris and several other cities imposed nighttime curfews Monday and Tuesday in certain zones prone to protests or looting.
Macron said that on Thursday he would chair a meeting of key ministers and intelligence officials to receive a “detailed account” of what happened last weekend.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who on Wednesday held a meeting with union leaders organizing marches, has vowed a “massive” police deployment for the fresh demonstrations called for Saturday by the Yellow Vest movement protesting rising inflation.
The convulsion in France, the EU’s second-biggest economy after Germany, has rattled financial markets already nervous about the country’s growing debt pile and deficit.
The yield on the French government’s benchmark 10-year bond has been rising, and on Wednesday surpassed five percent as investors demanded a higher return given the fiscal woes. A rising yield signifies a drop in bond prices. The Paris stock market also fell.
On Friday, the Moody’s ratings agency is expected to lower its grade on France’s public debt.
The country’s political landscape is so fragmented that Lecornu has little chance of winning swift parliamentary consensus for a cost-cutting budget that needs to be adopted before the end of this year.
The latest survey, carried out by Ifop in the wake of the riots, suggested Le Pen would lead first-round voting intentions by a wide margin and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon emerged as her most likely opponent in the runoff.
France’s neighbors Italy and Belgium have also started to experience similar unrest, on a smaller scale. Italy’s government has ordered 500 troops to Milan to stem street violence there.
Macron said that “we don’t need a state of emergency” that would likewise permit soldiers to reinforce police against rioters, adding that “we have the means” already at authorities’ disposal, such as curfews.
While the partial curfews have led to a calming of the situation in Paris and elsewhere, they have disrupted travel for commuters looking to take urban rail after 11pm (2100 GMT).
“It’s quite disconcerting,” said one Paris commuter who gave only his first name, Louis, when he found his line closed. But “if it can prevent further acts of vandalism... then yes, I think it’s a good thing,” he said.
The Yellow Vest movement behind last weekend’s demonstrations announced Wednesday it had formally told authorities it planned to hold its Paris march on Saturday starting from Bastille square.
The movement also wants to hold follow-up nationwide demonstrations on November 5.
The images broadcast around the world of France’s street violence last weekend have prompted several countries, including the United States, China and Germany, to issue travel advisories for their citizens in France.

The politics of othering
item.description:
While the state repeatedly pledges to uphold law and order, insecurity among minority communities remains palpable. Police records from 2025 documented 645 incidents involving members of minority groups, classifying 71 as communal and 574 as ordinary criminal offenses.
The Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council reported 257 incidents of communal violence in just the first six months of 2026, resulting in 44 deaths across 40 separate attacks.
While statistical discrepancies exist, the underlying reality is undeniable. Ensuring the safety, dignity, and equal rights of religious minorities remains an urgent national priority.
Against this backdrop, an even deeper question has emerged into public debate: Does the state have the authority to determine the religious identity of its citizens?
The issue reached a head on August 15, 2026, when the International Majlis-e-Tahaffuz Khatme Nabuwwat Bangladesh convened a National Ulama-Mashayekh Conference. The gathering culminated in a nine-point demand, chief among them that the Ahmadiyya community be legally declared a "non-Muslim minority."
Other demands included prescribing the maximum legal penalty for insulting Islamic sanctities, barring Tablighi leader Maulana Saa'd from entering the country, prohibiting his followers from holding the annual Ijtema, and banning the group Hizb-ut-Tawhid.
Jamiat Ulama-e-Islam Bangladesh President Maulana Ubaidullah Farooq has called on Hefazat-e-Islam to announce a parliament siege program this November if the government does not declare Ahmadis (Qadianis) non-Muslims. Similar calls were voiced at a Khatme Nabuwwat conference late last year.
These demands go beyond routine theological disagreement. They raise fundamental questions regarding religious identity, individual liberty, and the limits of state power.
Attending seminars organized by the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community in Bangladesh, conversing with their representatives, and reviewing their publications reveal a faith rooted in Islamic fundamentals alongside distinct theological perspectives.
The Ahmadiyya community firmly identifies itself as Muslim. Members uphold core Islamic principles: Affirming the absolute oneness of God, honouring the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), and following the Holy Quran.
At the same time, Ahmadi theology diverges from mainstream Sunni and Shia doctrines on specific theological points. Most notably, the community believes that Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian was the Promised Messiah and Mahdi , and holds a distinct interpretation regarding the death of Jesus (PBUH).
Despite theological differences with broader groups, the community emphasizes building harmonious relations across society.
Guided by their global motto, "Love for all, hatred for none," Ahmadi Muslims in Bangladesh actively promote peace, interfaith dialogue, and mutual understanding.
This philosophy of openness extends to their places of worship. The Ahmadiyya community welcomes anyone regardless of background or belief to visit their mosques across the country.
Representatives express a warm readiness to engage in polite conversation and address questions from anyone curious to learn about their faith and traditions directly.
While mainstream scholars view these doctrines as incompatible with orthodox Islamic theology, a critical line is crossed when a theological verdict is converted into a legal identity imposed by the government.
At the international level, Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights explicitly guarantees the right to freedom of thought, conscience, and religion, including the freedom to manifest one's faith publicly or privately.
Crucially, Islamic scripture and tradition also address the gravity of judging another person's faith. Surah An-Nisa (4:94) in the Quran warns believers: "Do not say to one who offers you peace (Salam), ‘You are not a believer.’"
The verse cautions against hasty declarations and urges careful verification.
This is reinforced by a well-known Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari , where Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) stated: "Whoever prays like us and faces our Qibla and eats our slaughtered animals is a Muslim and is under Allah's and His Apostle's protection (Bukhari, Kitabus Salat:384)."
Furthermore, while a tradition in Jami' at-Tirmidhi speaks of the Ummah eventually dividing into 73 groups (Tirmidhi:2640), it raises a poignant question: When theological differences inevitably arise, who holds the authority to decide which group is legally Muslim and which is not?
Pakistan offers a sobering case study of what happens when the state steps in to settle theological disputes.
In 1974, Pakistan constitutionally declared Ahmadis to be non-Muslims . Subsequent penal laws criminalized basic Ahmadi religious expressions, making it illegal for them to publicly identify as Muslims or use standard Islamic terminology. Minority Rights Group has extensively documented how codifying theological rulings into state law institutionalized discrimination and fueled systemic violence.
Bangladesh has already seen warning signs of such rhetoric spilling over into physical harm. In March 2023, a violent attack on an annual Ahmadiyya convention in Ahmadnagar, Panchagarh, left people dead, scores injured, and homes and properties burned.
Sociologist Pierre Bourdieu framed this dynamic through the concept of " symbolic violence ," a phenomenon where a dominant group uses institutional power to impose definitions and labels on a weaker group. When theological critiques are backed by state power, symbolic violence easily turns into physical disenfranchisement.
There is a vital distinction between theological debate and state-enforced identity. Religious scholars have every right to argue that certain doctrines conflict with mainstream Islam. However, the state’s duty is entirely different: Its obligation is to safeguard constitutional rights, maintain public order, and ensure equal citizenship for all.
This debate is not merely about one specific community; it touches on the foundational principles of the republic.
Who ultimately holds the right to define a citizen’s religious faith -- the individual, a dominant religious group, or the government?
How Bangladesh answers this question will define its commitment to human rights, freedom of conscience, and the rule of law.
The state need not become an arbiter of religious truth. Its fundamental responsibility is far simpler: To protect the life and security of every citizen while ensuring that theological disagreements never become an excuse for exclusion, discrimination, or violence.
Dilawar Hossain is a Research Associate at the Brac Institute of Educational Development . Rezwana Zaman Diya is a development professional.

item.title: The women are divine
item.description:
Among Bengali idol-makers, there is an old, informal belief, passed along by word of mouth - that a Durga is incomplete unless a handful of earth from the doorstep of a sex worker is mixed into her clay. The explanation given is that “a man who enters that house leaves his virtue at the door, so the ground there becomes pure.”
Whether or not every workshop still follows it, the idea deserves a slow reading. The goddess cannot be completed without the woman’s soil, and the woman herself cannot be admitted to the festival. The earth is holy; the person is not.
This October 2026, as pandals lit up from Khulna to Old Dhaka, the belief is worth asking about, because it states, in clay, how this society thinks about women.
Psychology has a name for the split. Freud’s 1912 essay, On the Universal Tendency to Debasement in the Sphere of Love , described men who can desire only a woman they have debased, and cannot desire the one they respect. It later became known as the “Madonna-whore” complex.
His diagnosis was about men, but the habit of mind is far older than his essay. Women were sorted into two boxes: “Pure” and “the fallen,” with nothing allowed in between.
Literature has always known it. Nathaniel Hawthorne branded Hester Prynne with a scarlet letter; Thomas Hardy subtitled Tess of the d'Urbervilles , “A Pure Woman” and then punished her for being human.
Our own Sarat Chandra gave us the sharpest Bengali version in Devdas. Paro, the respectable, forbidden girl, and Chandramukhi, the courtesan in whose house Devdas drinks himself to ruin.
Nazrul saw it too. In his poem Barangana , he stunned society by addressing a prostitute as “mother,” and asked who had the right to spit at her. He pointed out that the heroes and sages of our own myths had unmarried or “fallen” mothers. More than a century on, we still have not caught up with our national poet.
In life, and in death
Bangladesh is among the few Muslim-majority countries where prostitution is legal for adult women who hold a certificate, but the law is ambiguous, leaving sex workers vulnerable to harassment and prosecution.
In July 2014, around 1,500 women were forced out of the 200-year-old Kandapara brothel in Tangail. A High Court judgment in 2000 had called such evictions unconstitutional, but it was never implemented.
Newspaper reports have noted that sex workers are denied food, clothing, shelter, health, and education. When sex workers go to the police after being raped, they are ridiculed. Why? Because people cannot imagine a sex worker being raped. Many mothers send their children away, believing life outside the brothel will be harder because of stigma.
Even death is a denial. Locals refuse to organize funerals for sex workers, neighbours did not bathe her, and a local imam refused to lead her prayers. The only place available for sex workers’ bodies was a cremation ground.
In February 2020, Hamida Begum became the first sex worker in Daulatdia to receive a formal Islamic funeral. Until then, their bodies were often tossed into unmarked graves or the river.
Afterwards, the imam who led the prayers said he would not do it again, because villagers and shopkeepers had criticized him. The Sex Workers Network is still demanding equal burial arrangements.
The pedestal and the fall
A woman who must stay pure carries the family’s ijjat , its honour, in her body. And a stain, even one inflicted by someone else, turns the Madonna into the whore.
Look at who is made to hide. According to the Bangladesh Mahila Parishad, 786 women and girls were raped or gang-raped in 2025, up from 516 the year before while Ain o Salish Kendra counted 749 cases. Police headquarters recorded 21,939 cases of violence against women and children in 2025.
Between January and May this year, ASK recorded at least 118 children raped and 17 killed . In five recent high-profile cases, the victims were targeted by neighbours, relatives, or acquaintances.
Behind each number is a person who, in a society that has split women into goddesses and whores, now holds the “whore” half. Rape is generally branded as a stain on a woman’s chastity and honour more than as a crime against her body, which shifts the focus from the accused to the victim.
The victim is so heavily stigmatized that perpetrators use the crime itself to silence her. Society collectively ostracizes the victim and her family, which is why most rapes go unreported. Abusers justify the crime by blaming the victim; if she takes the blame, the culprit feels he did nothing wrong.
The same soil
In the soil story, men shed their virtue at a woman’s threshold and the ground holds it. In life, men shed their guilt at a woman’s threshold and she holds it. We bow to the clay goddess and then cannot bear the woman.
A society that calls women its mothers, then cannot bury them, cannot hear them, and makes the raped one hide her face while the rapist is shielded, has not forgotten reverence. It has made reverence a way to keep women in their place.
The idols are immersed. But the women are still at their doorsteps, and many are still hiding their faces. Divine in theory, dirty in practice.
Shuchi Binte Shahjalal is a member of the Editorial and Op-Ed team at the Dhaka Tribune and looks after the Trib Z and Arts & Letters pages.

item.title: ‘They hand you a weapon and say you don’t have to fight, just move back and forth’
item.description:
Mohammad Ali Hasan Sohel, from Goalanda upazila in Rajbari, is now in a hospital in Penza, a city about 700 kilometres from Moscow, the Russian capital. He has been receiving treatment there for one month and 10 days. Prothom Alo spoke to him over a video call yesterday, Wednesday.

Breaking down in tears during the conversation, Ali Hasan said, “Nobody wants a life like this. This is no life at all. I contacted the Bangladesh embassy, and they said they would try to help once I recover. But if I recover, they will send me back to the battlefield.”

Ali Hasan further said, “I don’t know whether I will be able to stand on my feet again within another year. I spend all my time praying to return home. Please, do whatever you can to rescue me and send me back to my family.”

Thirty people travelled to Russia together on 7 May to work as construction workers. Their families told Prothom Alo that they did not get the jobs they had been promised after arriving. Instead, they were sent to fight for Russia through deception.

At least 20 of them have died so far, while six remain on the battlefield. Two escaped from hospitals and returned to Bangladesh. The other two, admitted to separate hospitals, have appealed to be brought home.

The families of those killed and the injured said the 30 men were taken to a military camp and divided into three groups. Ali Hasan was among a group of 16.

Lured to Russia by promises of jobs, 54 Bangladeshis killed in war in 3 years

He told Prothom Alo that after just five days of training, five men were sent to the battlefield on the sixth day. They walked for miles, surviving on the dry food they carried, and reached a tunnel three days later. It was an underground military camp, where they were kept. Eventually, the remaining 11 members of their group joined them.

Ali Hasan said that, at one point, they were each handed a weapon, dressed in military uniforms and sent towards the front line one by one. Of the 16 men in his group, 14 are now missing, while the remaining two are in hospital.

Ali HasanThose who refuse to fight are detained, beaten and punished. Eventually, they are forced to go. They hand you a weapon and say you don’t have to fight; just move back and forth, right and left. It is bait, a death trap. As soon as you go, you come under attack from Ukrainian drones. Some are killed. Those who manage to return injured are taken to hospital for treatment.

“Those who refuse to fight are detained, beaten and punished. Eventually, they are forced to go. They hand you a weapon and say you don’t have to fight; just move back and forth, right and left. It is bait, a death trap. As soon as you go, you come under attack from Ukrainian drones. Some are killed. Those who manage to return injured are taken to hospital for treatment,” Ali Hasan said.

On 26 July, his wife, Akleema Khatun, submitted an application to the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment seeking her husband’s rescue and financial assistance for the family.

Deceived into fighting for Russia, Bangladeshi families now battle debt

The application said Ali Hasan had gone to Russia for a job to earn a living but had been deceived and ended up in the hands of the Russian military. Meanwhile, his family is under pressure from creditors to repay loan instalments.

Mohammad Palash Sheikh was also among the five men who went to the battlefield with Ali Hasan in the first group. One of his hands was blown off in a drone attack. He has been admitted to a hospital in Moscow for the past 24 days, according to his cousin Abu Saleh Islam, who spoke to Prothom Alo.

“Since he has lost one hand, they may not send him to the battlefield again. They will decide once he recovers. The embassy has also said it will try to bring him home after he recovers. Palash wants to return to Bangladesh by any means possible,” Abu Saleh said.

Tasneem Siddiqui, Founding chair of RMMRURussia must be made to cover all their medical expenses, outstanding dues and compensation. Arrangements must be made to bring them back to Bangladesh as soon as they recover.

On 26 July, Palash’s sister, Chumki Khanam, submitted a letter to the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment seeking his rescue and return to Bangladesh, along with financial compensation.

The letter said Palash, from Sadar upazila in Gopalganj, had travelled to Russia on 7 May in the hope of a better life, borrowing money and taking out high-interest loans. After arriving, he was deceived and handed over to the military through coercion and deception.

Bangladeshis sent to Russia for jobs, used as 'prey' in war, 20 killed: SRB

The letter called for diplomatic efforts to rescue him and financial assistance for his family to help ease the burden of debt.

Meanwhile, a responsible official at the Bangladesh embassy in Moscow told Prothom Alo that neither Ali Hasan nor Palash had contacted the embassy to seek repatriation, despite being injured in the war and receiving treatment in hospital.

The Russia-Ukraine war began in 2022, and Bangladeshis started travelling to Russia for work in 2023. The number of workers going there has increased severalfold over the past three years. Many end up being drawn into the war, largely as ‘bait’. Some have also been killed, although the exact number is unknown.

Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair of the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU), a private research organisation working on migration, told Prothom Alo that the Bangladesh embassy should take responsibility for the two men in hospital by contacting the Russian government.

“Russia must be made to cover all their medical expenses, outstanding dues and compensation. Arrangements must be made to bring them back to Bangladesh as soon as they recover,” she said.

item.title: Women lag behind in higher education and employment
item.description:
Girls outnumber boys at the primary, secondary and college levels. The picture changes, however, at university level. Excluding colleges affiliated with the National University, women account for less than 40 per cent of students at public and private universities.

Women’s participation in government employment after completing their education also remains below expectations, at less than 30 per cent. In other words, the progress girls make in the lower levels of education does not continue at the same pace in higher education and working life.

Education experts say girls’ participation in education has increased compared with the past. Greater awareness among families and guardians, expanded access to education and various government policy initiatives have contributed to this progress.

However, girls face a range of practical challenges when moving from secondary school or college to university and subsequently entering the workforce. Living away from home for higher education, a shortage of adequate accommodation, limited safe transport, family finances and marriage can all influence decisions about continuing their studies.

However, detailed research is needed to determine the extent to which each factor contributes to lower female participation at universities and to identify the necessary measures.

Similar considerations may influence women’s decisions about employment, particularly when jobs involve transfers, postings in remote areas, and concerns about safe accommodation and transport, as well as balancing family responsibilities.

These barriers do not affect all women equally. Nor should it be assumed that women’s underrepresentation in government jobs is attributable solely to family decisions or transfer policies.

Education experts say the progress girls have made in schools and colleges must be carried forward by ensuring equal opportunities in higher education and employment. This requires identifying the barriers that prevent women from pursuing higher education while also creating more women-friendly workplaces.

Setbacks in higher education

According to the Bangladesh Education Statistics 2025, published by the Bangladesh Bureau of Educational Information and Statistics (BANBEIS), girls account for 51.2 per cent of primary-level students and 54.67 per cent of secondary-level students. Their share at the college level is around 52 per cent. At the higher secondary level, girls make up 54.39 per cent of students in school-and-college institutions and 53 per cent in higher secondary colleges.

Bangladesh achieved numerical parity between boys and girls in primary and secondary education well before 2015 under the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). Girls’ participation increased further in subsequent years, but questions remain about whether that progress has continued into the later stages of higher education.

BANBEIS collects data each year on various aspects of educational institutions, including teachers, students and infrastructure, and publishes education statistics. According to its latest figures, public and private universities and the Open University together have more than 1.11 million students. Women account for 39.34 per cent of them.

Excluding colleges affiliated with the National University, the country’s 56 public universities had slightly more than 700,000 students, around 42 per cent of whom were women. Private universities had approximately 400,000 students, with women accounting for around 35 per cent. Female participation is therefore lower at private universities than at public ones.

The figures vary from one university to another. Women make up around 42 per cent of the more than 36,000 students at the University of Dhaka. At Jahangirnagar University, the proportion is around 49 per cent. Women’s participation is also relatively high at some medical and agricultural institutions. They account for around 55 per cent of students at Gazipur Agricultural University and more than 50 per cent at Bangladesh Medical University.

A gender gap in working life

Alongside women’s lower participation at university level, their representation in government employment also remains limited. According to the Statistics of Government Employees 2025, published by the Ministry of Public Administration, the country has 1,986,272 government posts. Of these, 1,464,350 are occupied, leaving approximately 525,000 vacant.

Of the government employees currently in service, 1,042,562 are men and 421,788 are women. Women therefore account for approximately 28.8 per cent of government employees, while men make up more than 71 per cent.

Women’s representation is even lower in senior positions. Of the 1,103 officials serving in Grade 1, only 162 are women, accounting for around 14.7 per cent. There are 206,973 officials in Grades 1–9, of whom 46,925 are women, or approximately 22.7 per cent.

c Large numbers of women work in the private sector, particularly in the garment industry and other sectors.

Action needed

Asked for her views on the overall situation, former caretaker government adviser Rasheda K Chowdhury told Prothom Alo that financial assistance, safe accommodation and transport should be provided to help girls enter university. The reasons they fall behind must also be identified and addressed.

She said equal opportunities must be ensured in recruitment and promotion in government jobs, while workplaces should be made more women-friendly. Creating opportunities for women to balance family and professional responsibilities would make it easier for them to enter the workforce and remain in employment.

item.title: Sajek blockade resumes, nearly 2,000 tourists stranded
item.description:
Nearly 2,000 tourists have become stranded while returning from Sajek Valley in Baghaichhari, Rangamati.

At around 9:00 am on Thursday, they were travelling from Sajek to Khagrachhari under the escort of army and police personnel. However, a blockade called by two regional organisations stopped them midway at around 9:30 am.

On Wednesday, Sajek Gano Odhikar Rokkha Committee and Sajek Karbari Association, two organisations, announced a third round of blockades on the Sajek tourist road. In a statement, the organisations said the blockade would continue indefinitely from Thursday. They urged all tourists to leave Sajek by Wednesday.

Following the blockade announced by the two regional organisations, the district administration declared Sajek closed on security grounds.

In a public notice issued on Wednesday evening, Rangamati Deputy Commissioner Nazma Ashrafi said the Sajek Valley tourist destination in Baghaichhari upazila would remain temporarily closed until further notice. The notice instructed everyone to leave Sajek safely by 4:00 pm on Thursday.

Following the district administration's directive, tourists began leaving Sajek on Thursday morning. However, just half an hour after leaving the valley, they encountered protesters at Ujobaazar in Baghaichhari.

Assistant Sub-Inspector Md Kawsar of Sajek police station told Prothom Alo, “We have received reports that vehicles carrying tourists have been stopped at Ujobaazar. We are currently unable to obtain updates on their situation because of network problems.”

Md Yasin, a transport coordinator for tourist vehicles in Sajek, told Prothom Alo, “On other days, vehicles carrying tourists leave Sajek for Khagrachhari at 10:30 am. However, because of the blockade, they left at 9:00 am today. Nearly 2,000 tourists left Sajek under the escort of army and police personnel. If nothing untoward happens, they are expected to reach Khagrachhari by noon.”

Earlier, on 15 October, activists of Sajek Gano Odhikar Rokkha Committee and Sajek Karbari Association launched a second round of an indefinite blockade on the Sajek tourist road from 6:00 am. They staged protests by setting fire to tyres and tree trunks at various points along the road.

One of the three demands put forward by the protesters is the withdrawal of armed members of the Parbatya Chattagram Jana Samhati Samiti (JSS-Santu Larma) from the Sajek area. They had called an indefinite blockade on 11 October over the same demand.

However, the JSS has denied the allegations. Sajib Chakma, the organisation's publicity secretary, told Prothom Alo, “These allegations are being made to divert attention from the longstanding oppression and harassment of ordinary people in Sajek by armed members of the UPDF.”

The blockade and the closure of the tourist destination have caused losses for local tourism businesses. Motijoy Tripura, joint general secretary of the Sajek Resort Cottage Owners' Association, told Prothom Alo, “Tourists have to leave Sajek because of the blockade. Many tourists have cancelled their advance resort bookings. When a road blockade occurs in Sajek, not only tourists and businesses but also local residents suffer greatly. People can no longer buy food supplies or transport locally produced agricultural goods to the market.”

item.title: Nearly 8000 children killed in road accidents in 6 years and 9 months
item.description:
Road accidents killed 7,963 children in Bangladesh between 2020 and September 2026. More than 31 per cent of them died in accidents while travelling to or from educational institutions.

Another 2,812 children lost their lives while walking along roads or crossing them. Three-wheelers caused the highest number of deaths among these child pedestrians.

The Road Safety Foundation revealed the figures in a report published on Wednesday. The organisation compiled the report using information from nine national dailies, 17 national and regional online news outlets, electronic media and its own data.

According to the report, 2,193 of the children killed were passengers in various vehicles, 2,812 were pedestrians, and 2,958 were motorcycle riders or pillion passengers.

Among the children killed as pedestrians, 1,271 died after three-wheelers (CNG-powered and battery-powered auto-rickshaws, Nasimon and votvoti) struck them. This accounted for 45.19 per cent of pedestrian fatalities. Heavy vehicles, including buses, trucks, covered vans and pick-up trucks, ran over or struck 1,126 children. Private cars, microbuses, ambulances and jeeps killed another 317.

An analysis found that rural roads recorded the highest number of child fatalities, at 2,713. Regional roads accounted for 2,082 deaths, highways for 1,974, and urban roads for 1,194.

By time of day, the highest number of children—2,634—died in the afternoon. More than 36 per cent of the children killed were aged between six and 12. The accidents also claimed the lives of 3,547 children aged between 13 and 17.

The Road Safety Foundation reported that 2,513 children died while travelling to or from educational institutions, while another 962 died while playing on roads near their homes.

The organisation identified several causes of child road fatalities, including road and transport systems that do not prioritise children's safety, drivers' lack of skills, underage driving and a lack of awareness about road use.

It recommended developing safer roads for children, raising road safety awareness among families and educational institutions, taking action against unskilled and underage drivers, and improving access to medical treatment for accident victims.

Road Safety Foundation Executive Director Saidur Rahman told Prothom Alo, “Rural roads run close to residential areas, and vehicles on these roads do not follow traffic rules and regulations. Law enforcement agencies are also absent from road monitoring. Children, meanwhile, do not know the rules of road use. The relevant government authorities show no concern about the issue, and there are no signs of growing awareness among the general public either.”

item.title: Man Utd humiliated as Arsenal deny Bayern in Champions League
item.description:
FBL-EUR-C1-COMO-MAN UNITED

Manchester United were hammered 4-1 by Como in the Champions League on Wednesday as the pressure increased on beleaguered manager Michael Carrick, while a late Declan Rice equaliser earned Arsenal a 2-2 draw away to Bayern Munich.

Elsewhere, Real Madrid thumped RB Leipzig 4-1 and there were also notable victories for Inter Milan, Aston Villa and Real Betis.

The most remarkable scoreline, though, came in driving rain on the banks of Lake Como, where United suffered their joint-heaviest loss in the Champions League in the last 30 years.

Nico Paz scored twice for Cesc Fabregas's Como, with Tasos Douvikas and Jacobo Ramon getting their other goals. This was a second 4-1 home win in this season's competition for the tournament debutants.

Joshua Zirkzee pulled one back at the death for United, but they are now seven games without a win in all competitions.

The Red Devils have just one win in the Premier League this season and have now suffered back-to-back losses in Europe. Carrick's position risks becoming untenable.

"I have not given my own position any thought," Carrick said.

"For us to play in that way, it's not acceptable. It wasn't a good performance at all," he admitted.

Last season's beaten finalists Arsenal have seven points from a possible nine after Rice struck in the 82nd minute to earn a draw in Munich.

Bukayo Saka went off injured early on but his replacement Eberechi Eze fired Arsenal into the lead, only for Alphonso Davies to level before the interval.

Harry Kane set up that goal with a magnificent pass and then gave Bayern the lead from a second-half penalty, his 10th strike this season in all competitions.

But Arsenal hit back as Bayern registered a second straight Champions League stalemate.

"We looked dangerous, we got the goal and we had a moment there where we could have killed off the game," Kane told broadcaster DAZN.

"Probably a draw was a fair result overall... There's a lot of games and we've got players with injuries, players missing tonight, so we take the point and move on."

Real three from three

Jose Mourinho's Real are one of five teams with three wins from three in this season's Champions League, as goals either side of half-time from Bernardo Silva and Arda Guler set them on their way at the Bernabeu.

Kylian Mbappe made it 12 goals in 12 games this season for Real before Tidiam Gomis pulled one back, but Yan Diomande completed Real's victory with a spectacular volley against his former club.

"We know every point is important to get into the top eight, we know we have to win as many games as possible -- we've won three and there are five to go," Mbappe told Movistar.

Villa also have a perfect record after three games, as they won 3-1 at home to Viking Stavanger with Ross Barkley's opener being followed by Emiliano Buendia's penalty and Henrik Heggheim's own goal.

Peter Christiansen got one back for the Norwegian champions who are still looking for their first win.

Inter had Alessandro Bastoni sent off midway through the second half before Carlos Augusto's late goal secured a 1-0 win at home to Shakhtar Donetsk, as the Italian champions got their first points.

Betis have maximum points as an Isco penalty handed them a 1-0 win over Feyenoord in Seville.

PSG blow

Club Brugge defeated Lens 3-0 in Belgium as Hans Vanaken, Joaquin Seys and Carlos Forbs all found the net.

Victor Osimhen sealed a 4-2 victory for Galatasaray away to his old side Lille in France, after earlier efforts from Yunus Akgun and Aleksey Batrakov and a Nabil Bentaleb own goal.

Teenager Soriba Diaoune got both goals for Lille, who have lost three out of three.

LASK of Austria have their first points after a fine 3-2 victory over Sporting in Lisbon.

Luis Suarez scored twice for Sporting, including an early penalty, but Christoph Lang, Sasa Kalajdzic and Krystof Danek all netted in between for the visitors.

Reigning champions PSG are top of the 36-team standings after beating Barcelona 4-2 on Tuesday, but the French side confirmed Wednesday that star winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia ruptured the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee in that game.

He will undergo surgery in the coming days amid doubts as to whether he will play again this season.

item.title: Fire destroys mosque, warehouses, shops in Gazipur
item.description:
A fire destroyed a mosque, several shops and warehouses in Sreepur, Gazipur, early Thursday.
The blaze broke out around 3:30am at the Sakhawat and Akhtar market complex in the No 2 C&B Bazar area of Channapara, within Sreepur municipality.
Four Fire Service units brought the fire under control after nearly two hours of efforts.
The fire gutted Rafiqul Islam’s sanitary goods shop, Falan Miah’s poultry shop, Shafiq’s textile scrap (jhut) and cotton warehouses, a scrap-metal shop and Baitul Jannat Jame Mosque.
Nurul Karim, station officer at Maona Fire Service, said they received information about the fire at 3:55am. Two units from the Maona Fire Service rushed to the scene and began efforts to extinguish the blaze.
As the fire spread rapidly, another unit from Sreepur Fire Station and a unit from Rajendrapur Modern Fire Station joined the operation.
The four units brought the fire under control at 5:48am, after nearly two hours of efforts.
No casualties have been reported.
The cause of the fire and the extent of the damage will be determined following an investigation, the fire service official said.

item.title: For harmony and worship
item.description:
The peaceful conclusion of this year’s Durga Puja celebrations across Bangladesh offers a powerful affirmation of our enduring ethos of communal harmony and pluralism.
From vibrant pandals packed with devotees to our leaders visiting numerous sites and being with the people to even the warm solidarity shown by the diplomatic community joining festivities nationwide, this year’s celebrations demonstrated the unbreakable bond of shared heritage.
Indeed, leadership at the highest levels, from Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visits to local pandals to President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir’s greetings urging youth to champion inclusivity, underscored a unified national commitment to protecting the rights, dignity, and security of every citizen, regardless of their religious background.
Crucially, law enforcement agencies reported no evidence of orchestrated conspiracies or malicious plots disrupting the festival. While there were some incidents that soured the experience for some in the country, what we take away from this week is that when the state enforces rigorous security and vigilance to thwart sectarian troublemakers, peace prevails.
For years, bad actors and dark political forces have sought to weaponize communal friction, manufacturing fear, and exploiting fault lines to fracture society - forces that persist to this very day. Yet, the overwhelming response of the public continues to be one of collective rejection toward those who peddle hatred and division, and long may it continue.
Diversity is not merely a demographic reality in Bangladesh but the bedrock of our national identity. As the festivities conclude, the collective resolve witnessed during Durga Puja must not fade.
The government, civil society, and ordinary citizens must maintain this unwavering vigilance, ensuring that secularism and mutual respect remain uncompromised throughout the year.
We must continue to foster an environment and be a nation where minorities are protected, traditions are honoured, and communal harmony is fiercely defended against any voice that seeks to tear us apart. This is the sign of true development.

item.title: Projects must be completed on time
item.description:
The stalled Tk9.33 crore drainage project in Shibganj, Chapainawabganj, is another example of how unfinished commitments can undermine the very purpose of development.
The 2.1-kilometre drainage project, intended to address waterlogging, has remained stalled for six months, with around 300 metres still unfinished. Disputes with local residents over the land required for construction have prevented work from proceeding.
Meanwhile, it is the everyday public that are left to navigate damaged roads, accumulated rainwater, and disrupted business activities.
A development project is only as valuable as the benefits it ultimately delivers. Yet, in Bangladesh, we continue to see public works announced, funded, and initiated, only to be left incomplete for months or even years.
Of course, disputes over land and residents’ concerns cannot simply be dismissed. Authorities must listen to affected people, explain the project’s requirements, and seek fair, practical solutions.
However, negotiations cannot become an excuse for indefinite inaction. Municipal officials must take responsibility for resolving the impasse and establish a clear, publicly communicated deadline for completing the remaining work.
This case raises questions about how public projects are planned and managed. Potential obstacles, including land disputes, should be identified before construction begins. Feasibility assessments, consultations with residents, and contingency plans must be integral to project preparation, rather than treated as matters to address after work has stalled.
Accountability must also extend to implementation. Authorities should regularly publish progress updates, monitor contractors against agreed timelines, and explain delays when deadlines are missed. Where obstruction occurs, officials must pursue lawful solutions instead of allowing an entire project to languish.
Every delayed project imposes costs on ordinary citizens, who lose time, income, and access to essential services while waiting for improvements that may never arrive on schedule.
Development must therefore be measured by whether the intended benefits reach the people. It's time to recognize that starting projects is a responsibility, but finishing them is an obligation.

item.title: Gold, silver prices drop
item.description:
The Bangladesh Jewellers Association (Bajus) has reduced gold and silver prices in the domestic market, with the revised rates taking effect at 10am on Thursday after raw gold and silver prices fell.
According to a Bajus notification, the price of 22-carat gold has been set at Tk226,400 per bhori, while 22-carat silver will cost Tk4,029 per bhori. The prices include value-added tax (VAT).
The decision was taken at a meeting of the Bajus Standing Committee on Pricing and Price Monitoring on Thursday morning, according to a notification signed by the committee's chairman, Dewan Aminul Islam Shahin.
Under the revised rates, 22-carat gold will cost Tk226,400 per bhori, while 21-carat gold has been priced at Tk216,240. The price of 18-carat gold stands at Tk185,800 per bhori, while traditionally made gold jewellery will cost Tk151,900 per bhori.
The price of 22-carat silver has been set at Tk4,029 per bhori. Meanwhile, 21-carat silver will cost Tk3,853 per bhori, and 18-carat silver Tk3,324 per bhori. Traditionally made silver jewellery has been priced at Tk2,508 per bhori.
Bajus said VAT is included in the stipulated retail prices and cannot be charged separately. However, buyers must pay additional making charges depending on the design of the jewellery.
When exchanging old gold jewellery for new pieces, a 12% deduction applies to the stipulated price, excluding making charges and the cost of stones. For selling old gold, the deduction is 18%. VAT cannot be deducted separately in either case.
The notification said the revised prices would remain in effect at jewellery shops across the country until further notice.

item.title: Body of fourth tourist recovered from Bay of Bengal
item.description:
The body of another tourist, identified as Harun, was recovered from the Bay of Bengal near Himchhari beach in Cox’s Bazar on Thursday morning, bringing the death toll from the incident to four.
Harun’s body was recovered from the Sagar Nibash area of Himchhari, a day after he and other tourists were swept away by strong waves and currents while bathing near the museum at Marina Resort on Wednesday evening.
According to local sources, a group of tourists were swimming near the museum when they were caught in strong waves and currents. As they struggled in the water, local residents rushed to help and managed to rescue several people.
Two tourists were initially recovered dead. Another was rescued in critical condition and taken to hospital, where he later died.
Two other tourists were reported missing. Harun’s body was recovered on Thursday morning.
The other deceased have been identified as Rohan, 23, and Shahidul Islam, 23. Rohan, the son of Mukarram Hossain, was from Diabari in Dhaka’s Uttara area. Shahidul’s address could not immediately be confirmed.
One of the missing tourists has been identified as 22-year-old Nafisul Haque Nibir, son of Nabibur Rahman, who reportedly lives in Dhaka’s Azimpur area. The identity of the other missing person has yet to be confirmed.
Beach staff member Mahbub Rahman said two people were initially recovered dead, while another was rescued in critical condition and taken to hospital, where he later died.
Ramu Upazila Nirbahi Officer Md Zillur Rahman confirmed that the tourists were swept away by strong waves and currents while bathing near the Marina Resort museum. He said local residents rescued one person alive and took him to hospital, while a search operation was under way for the remaining missing tourist.

item.title: Dhaka ranks 7th among world’s most polluted cities
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 7th among the world's most polluted cities on Thursday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 157 at 9:20am.
The air quality was classified as "unhealthy", meaning the concentration of pollutants in the air had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general population, according to the AQI scale.
Lahore in Pakistan ranked first with an AQI score of 294, while Delhi in India ranked second with a score of 235, followed by Jakarta in Indonesia third place with an AQI score of 174.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while 151 to 200 is classified as "unhealthy". A reading between 201 and 300 is considered "very unhealthy", while levels above 301 are deemed "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Maradona doctor was made 'scapegoat' for his death, Argentine court told
item.description:
A lawyer for Leopoldo Luque, a doctor charged in the 2020 death of Argentine football legend Diego Maradona, said in closing arguments Wednesday that his client was innocent and had been made a "scapegoat."
Attorney Roberto Rallin rejected the prosecution's argument that Maradona's November 2020 death was foreseeable, while another defense attorney, Francisco Oneto, maintained that his death resulted from an "acute and unpredictable" heart attack.
"There was absolutely no possibility of predicting this fatal outcome," Oneto insisted.
Prosecutors have requested a 12-year prison sentence for Luque, a neurosurgeon considered a key decision-maker for Maradona at the time of his death.
"We are here to proclaim Luque's innocence, not with television slogans, but with the evidence that supports it," Rallin said. "Leopoldo Luque has been the scapegoat."
Maradona died at age 60 from a cardiorespiratory crisis coupled with pulmonary edema.
He was found dead in his bed at a residence in Tigre, north of Buenos Aires, rented for his convalescence, following surgery for a subdural hematoma.
The death of Argentina's favorite son plunged the country into mourning in the midst of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Tens of thousands of people defied social distancing rules to bid farewell to him as he lay in state at the presidential palace.
A total of seven health-care professionals have been on trial since April for potential negligence leading to the star's death during his two weeks of convalescence.
Prosecutors have requested sentences ranging from four to 12 years for six of the seven defendants.
In its closing arguments, the prosecution condemned Luque's "inaction," saying his attitude "was always to do nothing" in the face of the warning signs that Maradona was exhibiting.
- Contested medical history -
Luque's lawyers particularly attacked the conclusions of the interdisciplinary medical commission, which had been established by the court in 2021 to provide an opinion on the star's death.
The commission, which based its findings on the autopsy and other things, said Maradona had a history of heart problems that should have been taken into account, a conclusion the prosecution emphasized.
But Luque's defense lawyers said that clinical tests done prior to Maradona's surgery just before his death didn't reveal any heart issues.
"It's so clear that Maradona didn't have any heart problems in 2020," Oneto said during closing arguments.
Throughout the trial, Luque was by far the most combative defendant, speaking several times when he felt he was being implicated.
His legal team played audio recordings, presented scientific articles and even a video of Maradona's autopsy, provoking the anger of the footballer's daughters.
"It's easy to attack me because I'm the one who had the most contact with Maradona," Luque said in court, asserting that "the only one who would defend me would be Diego."
"I cared deeply for him, I loved him, he was my idol and my friend," he said.
Defense attorney Nicolas D'Albora, who represents medical coordinator Nancy Forlini, also blamed Maradona's demise on Luque and another doctor, saying they "were obliged to guarantee the patient's health."
Forlini faces a 10-year sentence for homicide with eventual intent, for an alleged failure to provide basic medical equipment for home care.
The defense's closing arguments are expected to continue until Thursday.

item.title: Two matches, no 200: Bangladesh's batting problem a year out from the World Cup
item.description:
Bangladesh have a year left before the ODI World Cup, and the tri-nation series in the UAE has shown where the work lies: in two matches, their batters did not reach 200 either time.
Against Afghanistan on Wednesday, the top four were gone inside seven overs and eight of the 11 batters failed to reach double figures.
The 160 all out ended Bangladesh's hopes of reaching the final and gave Afghanistan their fifth consecutive ODI win over them.
Afghanistan chased the target with seven wickets and 87 balls to spare. They will meet Zimbabwe, who beat Bangladesh in the series opener, in the final in Sharjah.
Bangladesh needed to win by at least 41 runs to qualify after stand-in captain Towhid Hridoy won the toss and chose to bat. That meant keeping Afghanistan to 119, a mark they passed in the 27th over.
The innings was in trouble inside two overs. Tanzid Hasan edged Yamin Ahmadzai to wicketkeeper Rahmanullah Gurbaz, and Soumya Sarkar played on next ball, trying to cut a delivery just outside off stump. Najmul Hossain Shanto made 15 before he too was caught behind, and Hridoy was caught and bowled by Azmatullah Omarzai for a duck.
Parvez Hossain, called into the squad as Liton Das's replacement, and Saif Hassan took Bangladesh from 28 for four to 121. Saif, who scored at under a run every two balls throughout, was caught at midwicket charging Mohammad Nabi for 41 off 82 balls.
Parvez went on to make 70 off 96 balls, his second ODI fifty. Mehedi Hasan Miraz was dropped off a pull and caught two balls later playing the same shot, out for two.
Rashid Khan took four for 31 as Bangladesh lost their last six wickets for 39 runs. Soumya, Hridoy, debutant Aliss Al Islam and Mustafizur Rahman were all out for ducks.
Taskin Ahmed bowled Gurbaz and Sediqullah Atal inside the powerplay, but Afghanistan had already made 26 from the first 16 balls, 10 of them extras. Rahmat Shah's unbeaten 67 took them home in the 36th over.
The World Cup will be held in South Africa, Namibia and Zimbabwe next October.

item.title: Man Utd humiliated by Como as Arsenal deny Bayern in Champions League
item.description:
Manchester United were hammered 4-1 by Como in the Champions League on Wednesday as the pressure increased on beleaguered manager Michael Carrick, while a late Declan Rice equaliser earned Arsenal a 2-2 draw away to Bayern Munich.
Elsewhere, Real Madrid thumped RB Leipzig 4-1 and there were also notable victories for Inter Milan, Aston Villa and Real Betis.
The most remarkable scoreline, though, came in driving rain on the banks of Lake Como, where United suffered their joint-heaviest loss in the Champions League in the last 30 years.
Nico Paz scored twice for Cesc Fabregas's Como, with Tasos Douvikas and Jacobo Ramon getting their other goals. This was a second 4-1 home win in this season's competition for the tournament debutants.
Joshua Zirkzee pulled one back at the death for United, but they are now seven games without a win in all competitions.
The Red Devils have just one win in the Premier League this season and have now suffered back-to-back losses in Europe. Carrick's position risks becoming untenable.
"I have not given my own position any thought," Carrick said.
"For us to play in that way, it's not acceptable. It wasn't a good performance at all," he admitted.
Last season's beaten finalists Arsenal have seven points from a possible nine after Rice struck in the 82nd minute to earn a draw in Munich.
Bukayo Saka went off injured early on but his replacement Eberechi Eze fired Arsenal into the lead, only for Alphonso Davies to level before the interval.
Harry Kane set up that goal with a magnificent pass and then gave Bayern the lead from a second-half penalty, his 10th strike this season in all competitions.
But Arsenal hit back as Bayern registered a second straight Champions League stalemate.
"We looked dangerous, we got the goal and we had a moment there where we could have killed off the game," Kane told broadcaster DAZN.
"Probably a draw was a fair result overall... There's a lot of games and we've got players with injuries, players missing tonight, so we take the point and move on."
- Real three from three -
Jose Mourinho's Real are one of five teams with three wins from three in this season's Champions League, as goals either side of half-time from Bernardo Silva and Arda Guler set them on their way at the Bernabeu.
Kylian Mbappe made it 12 goals in 12 games this season for Real before Tidiam Gomis pulled one back, but Yan Diomande completed Real's victory with a spectacular volley against his former club.
"We know every point is important to get into the top eight, we know we have to win as many games as possible -- we've won three and there are five to go," Mbappe told Movistar.
Villa also have a perfect record after three games, as they won 3-1 at home to Viking Stavanger with Ross Barkley's opener being followed by Emiliano Buendia's penalty and Henrik Heggheim's own goal.
Peter Christiansen got one back for the Norwegian champions who are still looking for their first win.
Inter had Alessandro Bastoni sent off midway through the second half before Carlos Augusto's late goal secured a 1-0 win at home to Shakhtar Donetsk, as the Italian champions got their first points.
Betis have maximum points as an Isco penalty handed them a 1-0 win over Feyenoord in Seville.
- PSG blow -
Club Brugge defeated Lens 3-0 in Belgium as Hans Vanaken, Joaquin Seys and Carlos Forbs all found the net.
Victor Osimhen sealed a 4-2 victory for Galatasaray away to his old side Lille in France, after earlier efforts from Yunus Akgun and Aleksey Batrakov and a Nabil Bentaleb own goal.
Teenager Soriba Diaoune got both goals for Lille, who have lost three out of three.
LASK of Austria have their first points after a fine 3-2 victory over Sporting in Lisbon.
Luis Suarez scored twice for Sporting, including an early penalty, but Christoph Lang, Sasa Kalajdzic and Krystof Danek all netted in between for the visitors.
Reigning champions PSG are top of the 36-team standings after beating Barcelona 4-2 on Tuesday, but the French side confirmed Wednesday that star winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia ruptured the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee in that game.
He will undergo surgery in the coming days amid doubts as to whether he will play again this season.

item.title: Bangladesh crash out of tri-series after defeat to Afghanistan
item.description:
Bangladesh's vulnerable batting once again let them down as they endured a crushing seven-wicket defeat to Afghanistan, which ended their hopes to reach the tri-nation ODI series final.
Needing a victory by a margin of more than 40 runs to reach the final on net-run-rate, Bangladesh were bowled out for a meager 160 runs in 41.2 overs after opting to bat first at the Sharjah Cricket Stadium today.
Led by skipper Rahmat Shah's astute 67 not out, Afghanistan chased down the target in 35.3 overs, reaching 161-3 to seal their place in the final where they take on Zimbabwe on Friday. The Afghans earlier humiliated Zimbabwe by 158 runs in group phase.
Before suffering defeat to Afghanistan, Bangladesh tasted a 99-run drubbing at the hands of Zimbabwe.
Parvez Hossain Emon fought lonely to hit a career-best 70 to guide Bangladesh past 150 plus total which looked unlikely after a shaky start.
Legspinner Rashid Khan caused the most damage by claiming 4-31 but before his entry into the stage, Bangladesh lost half of the batting order by playing wayward cricket.
Pacer Yamin Ahmedzai dealt a double in just second over of the innings, dismissing opener Taznid Hasan Tamim for 1 and Soumya Sarkar for a duck in consecutive deliveries after Bangladesh captain Towhid Hridoy opted to bat first.
Both of the top order batters played loose shots to dig their own graveyards. To make matters worse further, Azmatullah Omarzai got rid of Najmul Hossain Shanto (15) and Hridoy for duck in three balls, leaving Bangladesh at a precarious 28-4 in seventh over.
Emon who replaced injured Liton in the squad to play his first ODI in more than one year tried to steady the innings alongside opener Saif Hassan who was watchful amid the top order's reckless show.
Together they batted with patience to mount a comeback but Saif too played a rash shot against Mohammad Nabi to be out for 41, ending a 93-run fifth wicket partnership.
Emon meanwhile reached his second fifty in fourth ODI and looked set to make it bigger.
However Rashid Khan sparked a collapse, including the wicket of Emon who smacked five fours and two sixes in his fighting knock as Bangladesh lost last five wickets for 39 runs.
Despite the modest total, Bangladesh had a narrow mathematical chance of defending it by dismissing Afghanistan for fewer than 119 runs.
Taskin Ahmed briefly raised hopes by producing two incisive deliveries, dismissing opener Rahmanullah Gurbaz (6) with a sharp inswinger before removing Sediqullah Atal (4) with another aggressive delivery to reduce Afghanistan to 39-2 in the seventh over.
However, Bangladesh failed to build on the early breakthroughs as Mustafizur Rahman and Shoriful Islam struggled to make an impact.
Aliss Al Islam, popularly called as mystery spinner in the domestic circuit who made his ODI debut, also went through a difficult outing by going wicket-less in his 8.3 overs spell that cost 47 runs.
Afghanistan captain Rahmat Shah guided his side towards victory with two useful partnerships-56 with Ibrahim Zadran who made 34 and 66 with Hashmatullah Shahidi, unbeaten on 36, to steer the side to victory.
Taskin ended with 2-36 while Mustafizur took 1-32.
