SSC test exam dates announced: Edu boards issue key instructions
item.description:
The test examinations for the 2027 Secondary School Certificate (SSC) and equivalent examinations are scheduled to be held between 28 October and 10 November.

The education boards have already published the notice on filling in forms for the SSC examinations.

It states that all students, except those retaking the examination after failing and those seeking to improve their GPA, must sit the test examinations.

According to the form-filling notice, the deadline for publishing the test examination results is 15 November 2026.

SSC form fill-up dates announced for 2027; six key instructions for candidates

Regarding the syllabus, irregular candidates and those seeking to improve their results will sit examinations based on question papers prepared according to the 2025 and 2026 SSC examination syllabuses.

Regular candidates will sit examinations based on question papers prepared according to the syllabus for the 2027 SSC examinations.

For students of all academic years, marks obtained through continuous assessment in physical education, health science and sports, and career education must be provided by the educational institutions to the relevant examination centres in accordance with National Curriculum and Textbook Board (NCTB) guidelines.

SSC students failing up to two subjects will be able to retake exams within 15 days: Edu minister

The examination centres will submit the marks obtained through continuous assessment online to the education board’s website, along with the practical examination marks.

The original handwritten mark sheets for the practical examinations and continuous assessments must also be submitted in person to the Secondary Examination Branch.

item.title: Canadian university launches USD 100m PhD scholarship
item.description:

item.title: Ambassador to stay away from Tokyo during PM's Japan visit, ministry secretary sent to coordinate
item.description:
During Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's visit to Japan from 26 to 29 October, Bangladesh's Ambassador to Japan, Md Daud Ali, will not be staying in Tokyo. It has been decided to keep him in Dhaka.

For diplomatic matters and overall coordination during this time, Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Bilateral Affairs), Md Nazrul Islam, has been sent to Tokyo with special responsibilities.

This information was confirmed to Prothom Alo by a high-level government source on Thursday afternoon.

According to diplomatic sources in Dhaka and Tokyo, Nazrul Islam arrived in Japan yesterday.

During the visit, he will be responsible for bilateral monitoring and diplomatic aid while staying in Tokyo.

On 15 October, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a letter calling Daud Ali to Dhaka for discussions regarding the visit. Following instructions to return within two days, he returned to Dhaka from Japan.

Several senior officials of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, on the condition of anonymity, stated that although Daud Ali was summoned to Dhaka for discussions about the visit, he was not involved in the preparatory activities for the visit.

Conversations with former and current diplomats have revealed that in the past few decades, there is no precedent for the absence of Bangladesh's ambassador during a prime minister's visit to an important country. They are also not aware of any instance where an ambassador in office was brought to Dhaka and given special responsibilities for a visit.

According to the itinerary, on 27 October, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will have a bilateral meeting with Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. The meeting is expected to discuss trade, investment, infrastructure development, and the implementation of the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA).

Both Daud Ali and Md Nazrul Islam are officers of the 15th BCS (Foreign Affairs Cadre) batch. Before becoming the ambassador to Japan, Daud Ali was Bangladesh's ambassador to Romania. He is scheduled to go on post-retirement leave (PRL) on 7 December of this year.

item.title: Microplastics detected in farmed pond fish
item.description:
• Microplastics were found in sediment samples from all 25 fish-farming ponds in Trishal.

  • Examination of 150 fish from six species identified 90 microplastic particles.

  • Sar punti fish had the highest levels of microplastic contamination.

  • Tiny particles of polyethylene and polypropylene were the most prevalent.

Researchers have detected the presence of microplastics in sediment and fish samples from ponds. The study indicates moderate to high levels of pollution in the bed sediment of most ponds evaluated.

While previous studies have highlighted microplastic contamination in river water, sediment, and wild fish—even identifying these minute plastic particles in river- and ocean-dwelling hilsa—researchers have now detected microplastics in Bangladesh’s aquaculture ponds.

According to the research team, this study is vital for understanding how these particles accumulate in fish farming ponds and enter the aquatic food chain through fish. The researchers claim this is the first comprehensive study of its kind focusing on bottom sediment and fish in Bangladeshi freshwater aquaculture ponds.

The study was conducted in Trishal Upazila, Mymensingh. Microplastics were detected in sediment samples across all surveyed ponds, as well as within the fish samples.

These findings raise fresh concerns regarding potential risks to fisheries resources, the environment, and public health, while bringing to the fore questions about how microplastics enter these ponds despite being cultivated in controlled environments.

The study, titled "Microplastics in Freshwater Aquaculture: Evidence of Sediment–Fish Transfer and Associated Ecological Risk in Bangladesh", was published this month in the Environmental Pollution, an international scientific journal.

Research across 25 ponds in Trishal

Fieldwork took place in Trishal Upazila, Mymensingh, a major freshwater aquaculture hub where commercial fish production relies on intensive and semi-intensive farming methods. Researchers collected samples from 25 selected fish farms during the winter season.

Professor Badiuzzaman Khan of the Institute of Environmental Science and Disaster Management at Bangladesh Agricultural University led the study.

He stated that this is the first study examining microplastic presence in freshwater farmed fish and could play a significant role in assessing potential damage to the nation's fisheries resources.

According to him, the primary objective was to determine the presence and characteristics of microplastics in pond bottom sediment and fish, alongside evaluating the relationship between fish morphological traits and microplastic ingestion, the chemical composition of the plastics, and the associated ecological risks.

These findings raise fresh concerns regarding potential risks to fisheries resources, the environment, and public health, while bringing to the fore questions about how microplastics enter these ponds despite being cultivated in controlled environments.

Microplastics generally refer to plastic particles smaller than five millimetres. These tiny fragments originate from the breakdown of plastic bags, packaging, ropes, fishing nets, and other plastic items, spreading into the environment from various waste streams and plastic goods.

Findings in pond sediment

The study revealed an average of 11.04 microplastic particles per kilogramme of pond bottom sediment. The Pollution Load Index (PLI) used to evaluate sediment contamination levels ranged from 1 to 4.5. Based on this index, researchers classified the majority of sampling sites as moderately to highly polluted.

Pond bed sediment can serve as a major sink for microplastics. Compared to flowing rivers, the limited water exchange in aquaculture ponds allows particles to settle and accumulate at the bottom over extended periods. Consequently, benthic (bottom-feeding) fish and other aquatic organisms in contact with sediment face a higher risk of exposure.

However, the presence of microplastics in sediment does not imply that all fish are contaminated to the same degree. Particle ingestion levels depend on fish species, feeding habits, habitat depth, and the overall pond ecosystem.

Examination of 150 fish across 6 species

Researchers examined a total of 150 farmed fish across six species, recovering 90 microplastic particles. The average concentration was 0.6 particles per fish.

Lead researcher Professor Badiuzzaman KhanFish are fed large quantities of commercial feed. We are not saying all feed is contaminated, but certain feeds do contain these particles. Additionally, floodwaters often carry microplastics from other areas into the ponds. We primarily detected their presence within the digestive tracts of the fish.

Ingestion rates varied significantly by species. Sarputi recorded the highest average at 1.2 microplastic particles per fish, while Rui and Mrigal averaged 0.68 particles per fish.

In contrast, the study noted lower particle counts in samples of Catla, Common Carp, and Pangas.

Regarding habitat depth, bottom-dwelling species accounted for 52 per cent of all detected particles. Species inhabiting the mid-water column accounted for 35 per cent, while surface-dwelling fish accounted for 13 per cent.

Mahbubur Rahman, Associate Scientist and public health expert at icddr,bThe situation has escalated to a point where microplastics are now ubiquitous. There is no proper disposal mechanism, and recycling is virtually non-existent. We have already detected microplastics in the human body; there is no guarantee that they will not reach humans through fish consumption.

Lead researcher Professor Badiuzzaman Khan noted, "Fish are fed large quantities of commercial feed. We are not saying all feed is contaminated, but certain feeds do contain these particles. Additionally, floodwaters often carry microplastics from other areas into the ponds. We primarily detected their presence within the digestive tracts of the fish."

Predominant types of plastic

Polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP) were identified as the primary microplastic polymers. Polyethylene is commonly used in plastic bags, wrappings, and packaging, whereas polypropylene is used in containers, packaging, ropes, and other plastic goods.

Researchers highlighted these polymers as indicators of potential sources linked to aquaculture operations and domestic usage.

Tiny plastic particles can enter ponds through fish feed, feed sacks and packaging, fishing gear, water supply pipes, and surrounding household waste.

However, the specific polymer types identified cannot be attributed to a single source. Confirming exact origin points will require separate sampling and analysis of these materials and incoming water supplies.

Why this matters

Trishal is a major aquaculture hub. According to the Upazila Fisheries Office, fish are cultivated in 22,000 ponds across the upazila, producing 72,000 tonnes of fish annually.

Senior Upazila Fisheries Officer Shahana NazneenPollution in fish ponds can occur due to poultry farming along the pond banks. We have already initiated enforcement drives and recently removed a chicken farm situated adjacent to a pond.

Senior Upazila Fisheries Officer Shahana Nazneen acknowledged the pollution occurring in these operations, stating: "Pollution in fish ponds can occur due to poultry farming along the pond banks. We have already initiated enforcement drives and recently removed a chicken farm situated adjacent to a pond."

Because the study was limited to 25 ponds in Trishal, its findings cannot be generalised to determine contamination levels across all aquaculture ponds in the country.

Mahbubur Rahman, Associate Scientist and public health expert at the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh (icddr,b), who has worked extensively on microplastics, told Prothom Alo, "The situation has escalated to a point where microplastics are now ubiquitous. There is no proper disposal mechanism, and recycling is virtually non-existent. We have already detected microplastics in the human body; there is no guarantee that they will not reach humans through fish consumption."

Health impacts

Concerns are growing regarding the health effects of consuming microplastics found in fish, alongside questions over whether high cooking or frying temperatures degrade these particles.

Professor Shimul Halder, Chairman of the Department of Pharmaceutical Technology at Dhaka University, told Prothom Alo that because polyethylene consists of complex molecular chains, standard cooking heat does not easily destroy it. As a result, microplastics can enter the human body via fish consumption, which he warned could adversely affect liver and kidney function.

Noting that the detection of microplastics in aquaculture environments is a serious concern, Professor Abdus Salam of the Department of Chemistry at Dhaka University emphasised that further research is essential to determine precise pollution levels, long-term impacts on fish, and the risks posed to human food safety.

item.title: 135 Saudi-bound flights cancelled, over 20,000 passengers stranded
item.description:
A total of 135 flights from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka to Saudi Arabia have been cancelled since October 10 following Houthi attacks on Riyadh and Dammam airports, leaving 20,672 passengers stranded.
Several airports in Saudi Arabia remain closed following the attacks, prompting flight cancellations on security grounds.
Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) spokesperson Kawser Mahmud disclosed the figures to the media on Thursday evening.
According to CAAB, the cancelled flights included 62 direct flights and 73 transit flights.
Of the direct flights, 23 were operated by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, 10 by US Bangla Airlines, 19 by Saudia and 10 by Riyadh Air.
The cancelled transit flights included 28 operated by IndiGo, seven by SalamAir, one by EgyptAir, 14 by Emirates, nine by Qatar Airways, eight by flydubai and six by Air India.
Kawser Mahmud said flight cancellations would continue if the situation did not return to normal.

item.title: 85 detained in addl DIG’s house raid sentenced to jail; liquor, one yaba pill seized
item.description:
A nearly three-hour police raid at a senior police official’s residence in Dhaka’s Bhatara led to the detention of 85 people, including 26 women, early Tuesday, with the detainees later receiving jail terms and fines through a summary trial.
Police seized liquor, one yaba pill and paraphernalia used to consume the drug during the raid at Additional Deputy Inspector General Abdullah Al Zahir’s house.
A team from the Detective Branch (DB) Uttara Division raided the 3-story house in the Additional DIG Abdullah Al Zahir Police Housing-1 residential area from 2:30am to 5:30am on Tuesday, following Monday night.
According to the seizure list, police recovered an empty 750ml bottle of locally produced Carew whisky, a 1-liter bottle of Indian Royal Stag containing about 500ml of liquor, and a 1-liter bottle of Smirnoff vodka containing around 200ml of liquor. A 1-liter bottle of whisky from an Indian company was also seized.
The list also included 1 yaba pill, paraphernalia used for yaba consumption, and a small amount of cough syrup residue known as Kush.
Several DB officials told Dhaka Tribune that the seizure list had surprised officials, particularly given the number of people detained and allegations of prolonged drug use and regular DJ parties at the house.
Following the raid, DB officials had said illegal drug use and DJ parties had been taking place at the house for a long time. They had also claimed that a large quantity of liquor, cannabis, yaba and paraphernalia used for yaba consumption had been seized.
The DB said the detainees were sentenced through summary trial. Each woman received 15 days in jail and a Tk500 fine, with an additional 3 days in prison in default of payment. Each man received a 1-month jail term and a Tk1,000 fine.
Al Zahir was removed from his duties and attached to Police Headquarters after the raid became public. He had been working in the Maintenance and Repair branch at Police Headquarters. His attachment to Police Headquarters effectively placed him in Officer on Special Duty (OSD) status.
The raid was led by Deputy Commissioner (DC) of DB Uttara Division Ilias Kabir. He said those detained had consumed liquor and yaba before the raid, leaving only the remaining substances recovered by police.
Kabir said parties had been organized regularly at Zahir’s house since 2025. Five of its 6 rooms were rented out through the online platforms Airbnb and Travala, while the caretaker occupied another room.
According to Kabir, the house, including the 5 rented rooms, was arranged to accommodate 10 people. It was rented out for Tk18,500 per day, with each partygoer required to pay an additional Tk600. Between 20 and 22 parties were held there each month.
Kabir said a man named Mahbub Alam received 30% of the monthly profit as commission, while the remaining 70% went to Zahir.
Earlier, Dhaka Metropolitan Police Additional Commissioner (DB) Shafiqul Islam had said the additional DIG rented out the house through online platforms and that tenants used it for drug-related activities. Of the 85 people detained, 26 were women.
DB officials said regular DJ parties were organized at the house, with invitations circulated through online advertisements. They said 5 bottles of liquor and a large quantity of synthetic drugs had been seized during the operation.

item.title: HSC results likely between October 25 and 29
item.description:
The results of the 2026 Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations may be published between October 25 and 29, according to a proposal submitted by the Bangladesh Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee.
Professor Syed Akhtaruzzaman, president of the committee and chairman of the Dhaka Education Board, confirmed the proposal to Dhaka Tribune.
A senior Dhaka Education Board official told the media on Thursday that results are usually published on Thursdays. As October 29 falls on a Thursday, the results may be announced that day.
The Dhaka Education Board also said chairmen of various education boards have proposed holding the next examinations within three months of the results being published.
The HSC and equivalent examinations began simultaneously across the country on July 2 under nine general education boards, the Bangladesh Technical Education Board and the Bangladesh Madrasah Education Board.
The examinations were scheduled to end on August 8, but some boards, including Chittagong, required additional time due to flooding. Practical examinations were completed by August 15.
A total of 1,270,583 candidates registered for the examinations under 11 boards, covering HSC, Alim, HSC (BM/BMT), HSC (Vocational) and Diploma-in-Commerce programs.
The examinations were held at 2,697 centres across 9,439 educational institutions. This year, the nine general education boards used a common question paper.

item.title: Bangladesh ambassador to stay in Dhaka during PM’s Japan visit
item.description:
Bangladesh’s Ambassador to Japan Md Daud Ali will remain in Dhaka during Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s upcoming visit to Japan, with Ministry of Foreign Affairs Secretary Md Nazrul Islam set to oversee preparations and arrangements in Tokyo.
Sources at the ministry said the ambassador would not accompany the prime minister on the visit. Md Daud Ali is currently in Dhaka on the instructions of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
However, a ministry official told Dhaka Tribune on Thursday that the ambassador was in Dhaka due to illness. Whether he would join the prime minister’s visit to Japan would be known after his leave.
The prime minister is scheduled to visit Tokyo from October 26 to 29.
According to relevant sources, Secretary Md Nazrul Islam will stay in Tokyo in the ambassador’s absence and oversee preparations and arrangements for the prime minister’s visit.
Nazrul Islam left Dhaka for Tokyo on Wednesday, October 21, to carry out the responsibilities assigned to him for the visit. He will remain there until the visit concludes.
According to diplomats, it is unusual for an ambassador to be in Dhaka on the instructions of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs ahead of a prime ministerial visit.

item.title: Man beaten to death at Dhaka hospital over child theft suspicion
item.description:
A 41-year-old man was beaten to death at Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital in Dhaka on suspicion of being a child kidnapper.
The incident took place in front of the hospital’s children’s ward around 11pm on Wednesday. Police have detained a man in connection with the incident.
Police said Md Alam Sheikh was loitering in front of the children’s ward when relatives of children receiving treatment there became suspicious of him and questioned his presence at the hospital.
As he allegedly failed to provide a satisfactory explanation, several people dragged him downstairs and beat him, leaving him critically injured. He died early Thursday.
Police said they went to the scene after receiving an alert through the national emergency service 999. Alam’s identity was later confirmed through fingerprint verification.
He was from Natore. Police have contacted his family members, who are on their way to Dhaka.
Deputy Commissioner of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Tejgaon Division, Ibne Mizan said the body had been sent to the morgue of Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College for an autopsy.
He said one person had been detained in connection with the incident. He added that legal action will be taken if the victim’s family files a complaint with the police.

item.title: Shibir says youth detained over PM comment is not a member
item.description:
Islami Chhatra Shibir has denied that Abu Bakar Siddique, 22, detained over a Facebook comment about Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to Rajshahi, is a member of the organization.
Imran Nazir, president of the Rajshahi metropolitan unit of Islami Chhatra Shibir, said: “There is an attempt to put the blame on Shibir whenever something happens. But Abu Bakar Siddique is not one of our members.”
Abu Bakar was detained on Wednesday afternoon at his maternal uncle’s house in Gholharia village in Hatrāmchandrapur, Paba upazila, Rajshahi. His father, Ainal Haque, was also detained during the operation. Both are now in the custody of the Detective Branch (DB) of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP).
Chandrima police station Officer-in-Charge Monirul Islam said police had found no information indicating whether Abu Bakar had previously been arrested or whether any case had been filed against him. His political affiliation was also unknown, he added.
Mahmud Hasan Limon, president of the Chhatra Dal unit at Rajshahi New Government Degree College, said: “I heard from people in the administration that Abu Bakar used to be involved with the Chhatra League. Now, apparently, he is involved with Chhatra Shibir. But I have not seen anything at the college. We did not really know him.”
Shariful Islam, an assistant professor in the History Department of Rajshahi New Government Degree College, said Abu Bakar was a regular student who had taken his first-year final examinations, although the results had not yet been published. He said he had not observed any misconduct by Abu Bakar at the college.
After learning about the Facebook comment, Shariful Islam spoke to several students. According to him, they said Abu Bakar’s father had previously supported the Awami League but had been associating with Jamaat-e-Islami since August 5.
Shariful Islam also said he had heard that Abu Bakar had been involved with the Bangladesh Chhatra League through his family, although he had not observed any such involvement at the college.
The Facebook comment appeared under a photograph of the prime minister posted by a page named “The Beauty of Rajshahi.” The account, bearing the name Abu Bakar Siddique, commented: “What a great opportunity. Only a sniper was missing.”
During his visit to Rajshahi on Tuesday, Tarique Rahman traveled on a Rajshahi University of Engineering and Technology (RUET) bus from the airport to Madrasa Maidan and then to Dharmasabha before returning to the airport. Large numbers of people lined both sides of the road to greet him, and he responded to their greetings.
Following the comment, law enforcement agencies launched an operation to identify the account holder.
According to local residents, a team from the Cyber Crime Unit of Rajshahi Metropolitan Police and Chandrima police station went to Abu Bakar’s house at around 2pm on Wednesday. He was not there, and his family members did not disclose his whereabouts.
At around 4pm, a team from SRB-5 arrived at the house in plain clothes. Unable to find Abu Bakar, the team detained his father for questioning. Ainal Haque subsequently told them that his son was staying at his maternal uncle’s house in Gholharia village.
SRB-5 members then took Ainal Haque to the house and detained Abu Bakar. A mobile phone used by the family was seized, and both were subsequently handed over to the DMP’s Detective Branch.
SRB-5 Commander Lieutenant Colonel Faisal Ishtiaq confirmed the handover, saying: “We have handed both of them over to the DB. They will provide further details about the matter later.”
Abu Bakar lives in the Kechuatail area under Chandrima police station in Rajshahi city. His father, a farmer, has 4 children, with Abu Bakar being the eldest.
On Thursday morning, Monirul Islam searched Abu Bakar’s house. After nearly an hour, police found no evidence worth seizing apart from the packaging of a pen drive.
Police also attempted to recover Abu Bakar’s laptop, but family members said he neither used nor owned one.

item.title: Six law enforcers injured as gunfire targets Sajek tourist convoy
item.description:
Six members of law enforcement agencies were injured in an attack on a tourist convoy amid a road blockade on the Sajek-Baghaihat road in Rangamati’s Baghaichhari upazila on Thursday morning.
The incident occurred in the Ujobaazar area, prompting the army and police to evacuate the tourists to safety.
Rangamati Superintendent of Police Muhammad Abdur Rakib disclosed the details at a press conference at his office around 2:00pm on Thursday.
He said the Sajek Gano Odhikar Rokkha Committee and the Sajek Karbari Association had enforced a road blockade from October 11 to 15. The programme was suspended from October 16 to 21 for Durga Puja, with plans to resume it thereafter.
The blockade left 2,933 tourists stranded in Sajek, the SP said.
To ensure their safe return, a convoy of tourist vehicles left Sajek around 9:00am on Thursday under the security escort of the Bangladesh army and police.
When the convoy reached Ujobaazar around 10:00am, law enforcement personnel held talks with the protesters to facilitate the tourists’ safe passage. The protesters then hurled bricks and stones at the security personnel, injuring six members, Abdur Rakib said.
The protesters were subsequently removed from the road, allowing the convoy to proceed.
Based on intelligence reports, authorities later learned that an armed group affiliated with the United People’s Democratic Front (UPDF) had opened fire targeting the tourist convoy, the SP said.
Law enforcement personnel returned fire to protect the tourists and safeguard public property, he added.
Intermittent exchanges of gunfire between the armed group and law enforcement personnel continued even after the tourists had been moved to safety.
The gunfight lasted from around 11:00am to 1:00pm, after which the situation came under control, Abdur Rakib said.
Md Jasim Uddin, a Mahindra driver on the Sajek route, said they left Sajek around 9:00am under a security escort.
“They were stopped by protesters at Ujobaazar around 10:00am and remained stranded for about 40 minutes. Later, security personnel dispersed the protesters using batons, allowing us to continue,” he said.
He said they reached Khagrachhari around 12:40pm.
Rahul Chakma John, organising secretary of the Sajek Cottage and Resort Owners Association, said around 3,000 tourists had returned from Sajek to Khagrachhari.
On Wednesday, Sajek Karbari Association President Natun Joy Chakma and Sajek Gano Odhikar Rokkha Committee Convener Babudhan Chakma announced in a joint statement that an indefinite road blockade would resume from Thursday.
The organisations alleged that armed members of the Parbatya Chattagram Jana-Samhati Samiti (JSS-Santu Larma) were active in different parts of Sajek.
They also alleged that the armed members had threatened and intimidated local residents, forced some people to leave their homes and seized mobile phones from villagers.
As a result, ordinary Jum farmers were unable to tend to their gardens, the organisations claimed.
They said the blockade would continue until the alleged armed members were removed from the area and measures were taken to ensure the safety and security of local residents.
Natun Joy Chakma said talks were underway with law enforcement agencies but they would not withdraw the blockade unless their three demands were addressed.
He said the blockade had been suspended from October 16 to 21 in observance of Durga Puja.
However, he alleged that the administration did not hold any discussions with them during that period.
He said tourists staying in Sajek had also been given sufficient time to leave, prompting them to resume the blockade as announced.
The indefinite blockade on the Sajek Road was initially launched on October 11 and suspended from October 16 to 21 for Durga Puja. With the blockade resuming on Thursday, concerns have resurfaced over tourist movement and security in Sajek.
According to local accounts, while the Bangladesh Army was escorting around 3,000 stranded tourists to safety, armed members of the United People’s Democratic Front (UPDF), along with women participating in the blockade, allegedly hurled bricks and stones at the tourists in the Gongaram Bazar area of Sajek.
The incident occurred as the tourists were being escorted out of the area amid the ongoing blockade.

item.title: Fire at Rangpur Medical College Hospital injures 40 patients
item.description:
At least 40 patients and their relatives were injured while rushing to evacuate Rangpur Medical College Hospital after a fire broke out due to a short circuit on Thursday morning.
The fire originated from a switchboard near the administrative section of the hospital’s electrical control room on the ground floor around 6:15am.
Firefighters quickly brought the blaze under control, but the hospital remained without electricity for six hours, triggering panic among patients and their attendants.
The power outage disrupted medical services, forcing the suspension of emergency surgeries and other treatments. Although partial power was restored to several wards after prolonged efforts, the nephrology, cardiology, gynaecology and kidney dialysis wards remained without electricity.
According to patients, hospital authorities and fire service officials, panic spread throughout the hospital as patients and their relatives rushed to leave the building. Those staying in wards on the second to fifth floors hurried down the stairs, with many falling and sustaining injuries. At least 40 people were injured in falls during the rush to evacuate the hospital.
As of 4pm, the offices of the hospital director, cardiology department, pathology ward, dermatology and venereology ward, kidney dialysis ward and nephrology ward remained without electricity, leaving patients struggling in the intense heat.
During a visit to the hospital, patients described the chaos surrounding the evacuation.
Shafiul Alam, a kidney patient receiving treatment in the second-floor nephrology ward, was being carried downstairs when his two nephews fell and were injured. Shafiul was also hurt in the incident.
At least 15 patients in the ward were injured while rushing downstairs, with some reportedly trampled in the crowd.
Several infants were also injured as patients and their attendants rushed down the stairs from the third-floor gynaecology ward with newborns.
Mamtaz Begum, a patient in the gynaecology ward, said her baby girl was born five days ago. After hearing about the fire, she rushed downstairs with her newborn and was injured during the evacuation.
Many others used the emergency exit stairs to escape, with several sustaining injuries in the rush.
Deputy Director of Rangpur Medical College Hospital Dr Md Abdul Mokaddem said the fire was caused by a short circuit.
“Efforts are underway to restore electricity to all wards,” he said.

item.title: ‘Amar Ekushey Book Fair’ to run from January
item.description:
The Amar Ekushey Book Fair, traditionally held in February to commemorate the martyrs of the 1952 Language Movement, will take place from January 7 to February 6 next year.
A notice signed by Bangla Academy Director General Mohammad Azam announced the dates on October 18.
The decision was finalised at a views-exchange meeting with representatives of publishers on October 13 at the Shaheed Munier Chowdhury Conference Room of Bangla Academy. According to the notice, the schedule was approved unanimously by the publishers’ representatives.
The meeting was chaired by Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury. Prime Minister’s Adviser on Cultural Affairs Dr Zahed Ur Rahman and Cultural Affairs Secretary Yasmin Begum also attended.
The annual book fair honours those who sacrificed their lives during the 1952 Language Movement and celebrates Bengali language, literature and culture. It also serves as a major gathering for authors, publishers, readers and literary enthusiasts from across the country.
The 2027 edition will begin earlier than the traditional February schedule, concluding on February 6

item.title: Rizvi: AL, covert group spreading misinformation against BNP
item.description:
Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi on Thursday alleged that the now-banned Awami League and a "covert group" were involved in spreading misinformation against the BNP.
"There are similarities in the behaviour and statements of the defeated forces and the group. As in the past, they are still spreading misinformation against the BNP," he said.
Rizvi was distributing awareness leaflets as part of a dengue prevention campaign organised by Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) in the capital's Shantinagar area.
He said the Awami League had long been involved in spreading misinformation and that another "secretive group" had now joined it.
"There is evidence of a kind of relationship between them. They themselves had said that they would forgive the Awami League," he added.
The BNP leader said propaganda had previously been spread portraying the BNP as a militant political party and claiming that people of other religions would not be safe if the party came to power.
The government, he said, led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had demonstrated that conspirators could not implement their plans if the government remained vigilant.
Rizvi said the BNP had contacted every Durga Puja mandap and held discussions with the concerned committees ahead of the festival. BNP leaders and activists had worked round the clock to ensure security during the celebrations, he added.
He also said many people from the neighbouring country had visited Bangladesh to attend the Durga Puja celebrations and praised the safe and peaceful environment during this year's festivities.
Rizvi said the BNP believed in transparency and acted accordingly.
"The BNP implements what it promises. The commitments made by the party before the election are being implemented sincerely since the government led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman assumed office," he said.
Referring to the distribution of Family Cards and Farmers' Cards, Rizvi said economists believed the initiatives could reduce the country's poverty rate by a further five percentage points this year.
He described the initiatives as an achievement of the government.
On the dengue prevention campaign, the BNP acting secretary general said leaflet distribution had resumed after a break of several days.
The campaign would continue to raise public awareness, protect people from dengue and reduce the risk of infection, he added.
BNP Joint Secretary General Advocate Abdus Salam Azad, Health Affairs Secretary Dr Rafiqul Islam, Organising Secretary Kazi Sayedul Alam Babul and Secretary for Volunteer Affairs Mir Sarafat Ali Sapu were present on the occasion.

item.title: The Climate Watch to deploy eight journalists at COP31
item.description:
As global attention turns to the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, Bangladeshi news organization The Climate Watch is preparing to bring South Asia’s climate struggles, demands and stories to the international stage.
Officially launched on November 3, 2024, The Climate Watch will deploy 8 journalists from Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka to cover the UN climate summit, scheduled for November 9-20. The team comprises 5 full-time journalists and 3 regional contributors, marking the publication’s largest international reporting operation to date.
While financial pressures have forced several established Western news organizations to reduce specialized reporting, The Climate Watch is expanding cross-border collaboration and investing in environmental journalism.
Founded in 2022 by award-winning Bangladeshi environmental journalist Shamsuddin Illius, The Climate Watch has developed into a regional platform connecting approximately 100 climate and environmental journalists.
“We are striving to become a voice for South Asia in global climate negotiations. Our countries are among the most vulnerable to climate change, and it is essential that we tell our own stories rather than rely solely on others to tell them for us,” Executive Editor Md Ibrahim Khalilullah said.
At COP31, its journalists will examine climate finance, adaptation, loss and damage, energy transition, biodiversity, displacement and climate justice, linking diplomatic negotiations to the everyday experiences of vulnerable communities.
The publication is also exploring collaborations with Shakti Foundation, Young Power in Social Action (YPSA) and Change Initiative to strengthen its coverage.
The Climate Watch’s investigations have examined deforestation, industrial expansion, groundwater depletion and environmental governance. An investigation into forest destruction around Chittagong’s National Special Economic Zone documented biodiversity losses, with its findings subsequently cited in public-interest litigation.
Its reporting has received international references from The Guardian, The Diplomat, Mongabay, The New Humanitarian and Fiji Sun, alongside academic citations involving Columbia University’s Climate School and the National University of Singapore.
Through its Birds in Climate Crisis initiative, the publication is producing 100 short documentaries on threatened birds, habitat destruction and changing ecosystems.
The outlet also contributed to Dark Side of the Boom, an Earth Journalism Network-coordinated investigation involving 14 newsrooms across 11 countries that examined the environmental consequences of digital infrastructure.
The collaboration received a 2026 Covering Climate Now Journalism Award, a Society of Publishers in Asia (SOPA) environmental reporting award and a special citation associated with the Osborn Elliott Prize.
Having covered COP28, COP29, COP30 and Bonn’s SB64 negotiations, The Climate Watch is also preparing to report on biodiversity negotiations at COP17 in Armenia.
Alongside its reporting, the organization conducts journalist training and pre-COP fellowships with the Center for Participatory Research and Development.
For the relatively young newsroom operating from climate-vulnerable Bangladesh, the COP31 deployment represents an effort to shift South Asia’s position in the global climate conversation from a region whose suffering is frequently reported by others to one increasingly telling its own stories.

item.title: When survival becomes a debt-financed affair
item.description:
Economic distress does not always announce itself through factory closures, unemployment queues, or empty markets. Sometimes, it reveals itself through a quieter transformation: Families continue working, shops remain open, salaries arrive on time, yet ordinary incomes no longer cover ordinary lives.
Parents reduce food purchases, postpone medical treatment, borrow from relatives, and exhaust savings to maintain familiar routines. The appearance of normality conceals a deterioration in economic security.
Bangladesh’s latest household survey offers a troubling account of this contradiction, suggesting that for millions of people, survival increasingly depends on money they have not yet earned.
According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics’ Living Standard Survey 2025, 47.42% of households borrowed money to meet daily expenses during the preceding year. The proportion reached 51.91% in rural areas, compared with 40.19% in urban areas and 32.11% in city corporation areas.
These figures deserve attention not simply because borrowing is widespread, but because of its reported purpose. Loans taken to expand businesses or finance education may generate future returns. Loans taken to purchase necessities indicate that present consumption has become difficult to sustain through existing income.
The survey identifies the underlying arithmetic. Average monthly household income stands at Tk 33,513, while expenditure reaches Tk 35,311, creating a monthly deficit of Tk 1,798. This difference may appear modest when expressed as a national average, but its implications are substantial.
The annualized gap amounts to Tk 21,576 per household, assuming the monthly deficit persists. For families already operating close to subsistence, such a shortfall can consume savings, increase dependence on informal credit, and leave little capacity to absorb emergencies. The average also conceals households whose deficits are considerably larger.
More importantly, the relationship between income and expenditure has changed. In the 2022 Household Income and Expenditure Survey, average monthly household income was Tk 32,422 against expenditure of Tk 31,500. Income exceeded expenditure by Tk 922.
The latest survey reverses that relationship. Although nominal household income has risen, expenditure has increased faster, suggesting that additional earnings have not translated into greater financial security.
The figures do not establish why every household is borrowing, nor do they reveal the distribution of deficits. Nevertheless, they identify a structural warning: Rising incomes mean little when the purchasing power they represent is insufficient to sustain consumption.
This distinction challenges a common assumption in economic debate: That an increase in nominal earnings necessarily indicates improved welfare. What matters is the relationship between income, prices, and essential needs.
If wages rise by less than the cost of food, housing, transport, and healthcare, workers become poorer in practical terms without necessarily receiving smaller pay packets. Their nominal income may increase while their real choices contract.
They can continue buying necessities only by reducing quality, sacrificing other needs or borrowing. Economic insecurity thus develops not only through income loss but also through the gradual disappearance of affordable alternatives.
Bangladesh’s wage and inflation figures reinforce this interpretation. Government data indicate that inflation exceeded wage growth for 56 consecutive months through September 2026. Meanwhile, annual wage growth slowed from 8.05% in August to 7.9% in September. These figures suggest that workers have endured a prolonged erosion of purchasing power.
However, the national averages should be interpreted carefully: Households differ in their employment, earnings, and consumption patterns, while inflation affects expenditure categories unevenly. Lower-income families are particularly vulnerable because food and other necessities absorb a larger share of their budgets, leaving less room to adjust when prices rise.
The consequences become clearer when regional differences are examined. Average monthly household expenditure is Tk 46,778 in city corporation areas, Tk 37,344 in other urban areas, and Tk 32,532 in rural areas. Yet rural households report the highest incidence of borrowing.
This apparent contradiction disappears once expenditure levels are distinguished from economic capacity. Urban households may spend more because housing, transportation, and services are expensive. Rural households may spend less because their incomes are lower and their consumption is already constrained.
Lower expenditure, therefore, cannot automatically be interpreted as greater affordability. It may instead reflect deprivation that household averages fail to capture.
The composition of expenditure also matters. Rural families devote relatively more of their budgets to food, while non-food items account for 56.7% of household expenditure in city corporation areas.
These patterns expose different dimensions of vulnerability. When food prices rise, rural households have limited scope to reduce an already essential expense. Urban families face pressure from rent, transport, education, and healthcare, costs that are often difficult to avoid.
Consequently, identical inflation rates can produce unequal hardships. Effective economic policy must account for these differences rather than treating households as interchangeable units in a national average.
Rural indebtedness also reflects differences in employment opportunities and income stability. Agricultural earnings can be seasonal, while informal employment frequently provides neither predictable wages nor protection against illness and unemployment.
Remittances support many communities, but their benefits do not reach every household. Families without stable employment, migrant earners, or adequate savings may have few alternatives when essential expenses exceed income.
Borrowing bridges the immediate gap without correcting its cause. If the next month’s earnings remain insufficient, repayment becomes another expense competing with food, healthcare, and education. What begins as temporary assistance can become a recurring mechanism for financing poverty.
This is why the distinction between productive and distress borrowing is essential. Credit can help households acquire assets, establish businesses, and improve their future earning capacity.
Borrowing for consumption is not necessarily harmful when it addresses a temporary disruption and repayment is affordable. The danger arises when loans repeatedly finance unavoidable expenditure without a credible prospect of higher income.
In such circumstances, debt does not smooth consumption across time; it transfers deprivation into the future. Interest payments may then deepen the original shortfall, while the absence of savings makes households increasingly vulnerable to economic shocks.
The wider economic environment compounds this pressure. The World Bank’s Bangladesh Development Update, released on October 6, warned that prolonged economic weakness, inadequate labour demand and persistent inflation were undermining living standards.
It projected that the national poverty rate could rise from 18.7% in 2022 to 22.5% in 2026. This is a projection, not a confirmed outcome, but it signals a serious risk.
The energy crisis adds another constraint by increasing production difficulties, reducing operating hours and discouraging recruitment. When businesses cannot expand employment, households lose opportunities to compensate for rising prices through additional earnings.
These pressures reveal a limitation in judging economic performance primarily through aggregate growth. Growth can coexist with declining household security when its benefits are unevenly distributed, employment creation is inadequate or real wages stagnate.
The survey alone cannot establish the precise contribution of each factor, but its findings, considered alongside wage and inflation data, suggest that economic recovery cannot be assessed solely by the movement of headline indicators. The decisive question is whether growth generates reliable incomes and whether those incomes preserve people’s ability to meet essential needs without sacrificing their future.
The human consequences extend beyond material deprivation. Financial insecurity forces families to make decisions that rarely appear in economic statistics. A parent may postpone a child’s education, an elderly person may delay treatment, or a worker may continue an exhausting job because losing even one month’s income would be disastrous.
Such compromises gradually diminish opportunity and dignity. Children growing up in financially strained households may inherit disadvantages through poorer nutrition, interrupted education, and reduced access to healthcare. Household debt can therefore transmit present economic weakness into future inequality, making recovery more difficult across generations.
The government must respond with a combination of immediate protection and structural reform. Controlling inflation requires credible macroeconomic management, stronger competition in essential commodity markets and action against practices that unnecessarily increase prices.
Employment policy must encourage productive investment, reliable energy supply, and the creation of decent-paying jobs. Wage adjustments should reflect actual living costs, particularly for vulnerable workers, while targeted social assistance should protect households unable to absorb further shocks.
Better income and expenditure data would also help identify which groups face the largest deficits and whether interventions improve their circumstances.
The Ninth National Pay Scale provides one immediate policy context because the National Pay Commission commissioned the BBS survey to inform its recommendations. Public employees’ purchasing power deserves consideration, but cannot resolve a wider crisis affecting private-sector workers, informal labourers, and rural households.
Poorly calibrated increases could also create additional fiscal pressures without addressing the causes of inflation. The challenge is to protect workers’ real incomes while strengthening productivity, employment, and price stability. A credible response must recognize that household welfare depends on both what people earn and what their earnings can actually buy.
Ultimately, the most revealing measure of economic progress is not simply how much money enters a household, but whether that money provides security. When nearly half of households report borrowing for daily expenses, the issue extends beyond individual financial management.
It raises questions about wages, employment, prices, and the distribution of economic opportunity. Debt used to build a future can represent investment; debt repeatedly used to purchase necessities signals that the present is becoming unaffordable.
Bangladesh must confront this distinction before borrowing becomes an ordinary condition of family life, and financial insecurity becomes an inherited feature of poverty.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.title: Vladimir Putin seems to have Donald Trump exactly where he wants him
item.description:
Four weeks after signing into law new sanctions on Russia, Donald Trump has stunned even some of his own Republican colleagues.
The US president has given his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, his biggest economic and propaganda victory since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Even Putin, a man who built his career understanding the psychology of people so he could recruit them to spy for the KGB, must have been stunned by this Trump about-turn.
It was only in September that Trump signed new sanctions on Russia’s energy sector, which were championed by the late senator Lindsey Graham and named in his honor.
Now he’s done a deal with Putin for Russia to supply diesel to the “American and global marketplace.”
The diesel deal undercuts US efforts to create enough economic pain to force Putin to end the war.
After all, if Ukraine unilaterally decided to put down its guns now, it would lose the one-fifth of land the Russians have taken and risk losing the entire country. But if Russia were to put down its weapons, the war would stop.
Trump has done this deal for base political reasons; the high cost of diesel, largely due to the war in Iran, is one reason Republicans are battling to retain control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate at the midterm elections.
“We have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine,” Trump said this week. “We’ve got nothing back other than high diesel.”
Leading Republicans and Democrats argue that it’s not about Washington “getting nothing back,” rather, they argue, if Putin is allowed to conquer Ukraine he will be rewarded for an illegal invasion and may then turn his focus to other countries in Europe.
“It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Republican senator Thom Tillis said.
Trump is sending other signals that he has decided to embrace Russia.
He has said he was interested in Moscow’s proposal for a summit between the US, China and Russia. Apart from elevating Putin, it would involve discussion about a war with one side — the country that has been attacked not in the room.
Then came the description this week of Putin by Steve Witkoff, Trump’s Ukraine war negotiator, as a “humanitarian,” following Russia’s release of an American it had held in prison for four years. For the families of the thousands of Ukrainian civilians killed by Putin’s missiles, that word would be difficult to digest.
Another revelation in recent days was that either Elon Musk or the White House had ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink relied on by Ukraine.
When President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said people could die because of the change, Musk placed the blame with Trump.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus,” he wrote on X.
Trump retorted that he didn’t know who was responsible, but he would “like to find out.”
The Wall Street Journal found out for him, reporting this week it was Musk who had limited Ukraine’s access to signals which help it to fight the war.
Some US officials, cited by the newspaper, said Musk acted “unilaterally” and Trump “didn’t specifically order any retribution against Ukraine”. But one person familiar with the situation, the paper reported, said “Musk talked to multiple senior administration officials, including with Trump, before imposing the new speed cap.”
Even if it was Musk’s decision, he obviously felt confident enough that Trump, with whom he appears to be back in regular contact, would not have a problem with the decision.
Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican congressman on the House of Representatives Oversight Committee, told CNN it would be impossible for Musk to change a military-grade version of Starlink without the US military knowing.
“Ukraine is the victim here, Russia is the aggressor, Ukraine is our ally,” he said, describing the situation as “heartbreaking.”
For Putin, this is a huge victory. Regardless of who ordered the downgrading, Ukraine was being weakened.
Trump is delivering for Putin a festival of propaganda. Along with his big new diesel deal with the US, Putin can announce to Russians that Trump is considering a three-way summit with him and China’s president, Xi Jinping.
Putin could not be scripting this better.
But for young Russians who have had to endure the horror of one of the world’s longest frontlines, these days are grim.
Actual numbers are not available, but Russian casualties, including deaths, injuries and those missing, are widely believed to be as high as 1 million.
Putin, a man trained by the KGB to play mind games, seems to have Trump exactly where he wants him.
Those mind games began immediately upon Trump’s second term. Two days after Trump was re-elected, Russia’s most-watched television network carried reports “welcoming” Trump back to the White House, complete with a series of naked photographs of Melania Trump.
Nothing sensitive appears on the Russia 1 Channel that Putin or his enforcers do not want. The montage of nude photographs, while presenters were reading words of congratulations, was the sort of thing a Mafia boss would do: speaking kind words while at the same time showing images that suggested a certain menace or humiliation.
That apparent warning shot was the latest in the psychodrama that Putin has had with four other US presidents: Bill Clinton, George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden.
Each president entered the Oval Office hoping to be able to form a good relationship with Putin, to tame what they saw as the potentially dangerous Russian bear. But each ended up bitterly disappointed with the reality of their dealings with Putin.
With Trump, Putin surely must have realized that few world leaders were as obviously open to flattery as the US president, which would make the task of someone wanting to win him over so much easier.
Trump’s style has long appealed to Putin. Stephen Hadley, US national security adviser for four years from 2005, told PBS Frontline that Putin saw Trump as having a “penchant for authoritarianism” and “a backing off of human rights.”
“What’s not to like if you’re Vladimir Putin? It sort of sounds like he’s one of us,” Hadley said.
Trump wants Ukraine to agree that Russia keeps the current land it has taken since 2022. Zelenskyy has agreed to that, saying he would consider agreeing to a ceasefire based on the current frontline being frozen.
But Russia wants more. It wants the entire Donbas area.
Despite the fact that it is Russia which both invaded and does not want to end this war, Trump keeps rewarding the country.
Based on all the available evidence, it would appear that Putin has outmanoeuvred yet another US president.

item.title: Two dead in eastern Saudi airport attack
item.description:
A late-night attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport killed two people and injured eight others, the civil aviation authority said on Thursday, as strikes by Yemen’s Houthis intensify.
A Saudi and an Indian man were killed in the attack on Wednesday, the general authority of civil aviation said in a statement, updating an earlier death toll. Damage to the airport was being assessed, it added.
On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted and destroyed a drone in the Riyadh region.
In recent weeks, Houthi attacks on Saudi oil and civilian infrastructure have reached an unprecedented scale, forcing Riyadh to shut its main airport and postpone a major investment conference.
A total of 22 people have been killed in attacks on Saudi airports this month, according to an AFP tally of official figures.
A Houthi maritime blockade in the Red Sea is also threatening oil shipments from Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest exporter of crude.
The Houthi attacks follow the collapse in July of a years-long truce in Yemen’s civil war, where the Iran-backed group is fighting the government supported by the Saudi-led coalition.
The Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before launching a major offensive in September in which they seized Yemeni government-held territory along the Red Sea coast.
In response, the Saudi air force has frequently targeted areas under Houthi control, which include much of impoverished Yemen.

item.title: Harry Styles debuts unreleased song in tribute to Liam Payne
item.description:
Harry Styles has performed an unreleased song written in memory of his former One Direction bandmate Liam Payne during a concert at New York’s Madison Square Garden.
Titled “What Is Enough”, the track was performed on the second anniversary of Payne’s death. The singer died in October 2024 after falling from a hotel balcony in Buenos Aires, Argentina.
Addressing the audience during his “Together, Together” tour residency in New York, Styles reflected on the loss of his friend and former colleague.
“There are so many people in my life, friends and people that I've worked with that I wouldn't have been able to do this without,” Styles said. “And two years ago today, I lost one of those friends.”
Before performing the acoustic track, the singer urged fans to support one another through grief and difficult times.
“I'm sure a lot of you have been through similar things,” he added. “Really, it's just about looking after each other.”
Styles and Payne rose to global fame alongside Niall Horan, Louis Tomlinson and Zayn Malik as members of One Direction. The group was formed on The X Factor in 2010 and became one of the most successful boy bands of its generation.
Following the group’s hiatus in 2016, Styles established a successful solo career, earning multiple Grammy Awards. His album Harry’s House won Album of the Year at the 2023 Grammy Awards.
The unreleased song’s debut offered a personal moment of remembrance for Payne, bringing the singer’s legacy into focus during Styles’ New York performance.

item.title: Netflix partners with ‘Hoichoi’ to bring Bengali hits to wider audience
item.description:
Netflix has partnered with Bengali-first streaming platform and content studio Hoichoi to bring acclaimed series, upcoming releases and original productions to audiences across India.
Under the agreement, all Hoichoi series premiering over the next two years will be available exclusively on Netflix in Hindi, Tamil and Telugu, expanding the reach of Bengali storytelling beyond its traditional-language audience.
The partnership will bring several popular Hoichoi titles to Netflix, including Ashfaque Nipun’s acclaimed series Mohanagar and Amitabh Reza Chowdhury’s Bohemian Ghora, also known as Shaadi Ka Siyappa .
Other titles joining Netflix’s catalogue include Madam Inspector, Sampurna, Lojja, Eken, Anjaan Saaye, The Curse of Parnashavari, Bloodlines, The Adventures of Daadi & Jagga, Raat Abhi Baaki Hain, Achinta: Trial By Law, Queens and Parineeta: A Love Story .
The collaboration will also bring new Hoichoi productions to Netflix in Hindi, Tamil and Telugu alongside their Bengali premieres on Hoichoi.
Leading the upcoming lineup is The Cursed Temple of Kauriburi , a folklore-inspired horror series starring Jeetu Kamal, Solanki Roy and Paoli Dam. The series is scheduled to premiere on November 6, with additional titles set to follow in the coming months.
The partnership marks a significant step in bringing Bengali-language stories to a broader Indian audience through multilingual streaming releases, while giving viewers access to a wider selection of Hoichoi’s established and upcoming productions

item.title: Matthew McConaughey sparks 2028 presidential speculation with call for independent candidates
item.description:
Oscar-winning actor Matthew McConaughey has reignited speculation about a possible run for the US presidency in 2028 after releasing a six-minute video urging voters to give independent candidates a greater role in American politics.
Released on October 18, ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, the video encourages voters to take independent candidates seriously rather than dismiss them as protest candidates or spoilers. McConaughey, however, did not announce any plans to run for office or endorse a candidate or political party.
“Independent does not mean you’re middle of the road. Independent is the original road,” he said, presenting political independence as an alternative to the traditional Republican-Democratic divide.
According to The Telegraph, McConaughey also argued that independently elected representatives could encourage compromise in a closely divided Congress and hold both major parties accountable. He urged voters to examine candidates’ positions and determine whether their views aligned with their own beliefs.
The video has prompted renewed discussion about the actor’s political ambitions, although McConaughey has neither confirmed nor ruled out a presidential bid.
His potential entry into politics has been a subject of speculation for several years. In 2021, he considered running for governor of Texas but ultimately decided against entering the race. In July 2024, he described himself as being on a “learning tour” while exploring the possibility of public office. He later said he would not pursue a political campaign at that time.
McConaughey’s latest remarks have also attracted criticism from commentators and social media users who questioned whether independent candidates could split the vote and influence closely contested elections.
The discussion comes amid growing identification with political independence in the United States. According to Gallup, 45% of Americans identified as political independents in 2025, a record high at the time.
For now, McConaughey’s video has renewed questions about his political future, but the actor has yet to announce any plans to enter the 2028 presidential race.

item.title: Gazipur’s ‘Ulka cinema hall’ to shut down in November
item.description:
Ulka, a long-running single-screen cinema hall at Gazipur Chowrasta, is set to close permanently in November as falling attendance, mounting losses and rising operating costs make it increasingly difficult to keep the business afloat.
Mohammad Rafiq Uddin, managing director of the cinema hall, confirmed the decision, saying ticket sales from current releases are no longer sufficient to cover even electricity bills.
“The hall is struggling to survive. We are incurring losses continuously. The films currently screening cannot even cover the electricity bill,” he said.
Rafiq Uddin said films with compelling stories and established stars continue to attract audiences. However, relying on releases concentrated around the two Eid festivals is not enough to sustain a cinema hall throughout the year.
He pointed to the audience response to films starring Shakib Khan, suggesting that more releases featuring the actor outside the Eid seasons could help single-screen cinemas remain viable.
Unusually high electricity bills have added to the financial strain, according to Rafiq Uddin. With operating expenses becoming increasingly difficult to manage, the owners have decided to shut down rather than continue accumulating losses.
Audience numbers have also declined sharply, hall authorities said. Some screenings attract only a handful of moviegoers, leaving ticket revenue insufficient to cover staff salaries and routine operating expenses.
The planned closure comes as Kamruzzaman’s Sneher Bondhon is screening at the venue. Starring Joy Chowdhury and Mou Khan, the film was released in 14 cinemas on October 16.
Its promotional campaign included appearances on an open-roof bus in Dhaka. However, reports from the exhibition circuit indicate that the film has struggled to attract audiences.
The closure will further narrow cinema-going options in Gazipur, an industrial district with a large working population. Local industry sources said four cinemas were operating in the district around a year to 18 months ago.
Once Ulka closes, only Barsha and Jhumur cinemas are expected to remain open in the district. Both venues are reportedly facing financial difficulties, raising further concerns about the future of single-screen cinema in the area.
Ulka’s shutdown highlights the challenges facing traditional cinema halls in Bangladesh, where declining attendance and rising operating costs continue to put pressure on venues that have long provided relatively affordable big-screen entertainment.

item.title: Chiranjit Biswas wins ‘Best Male Actor’ at Tasveer Film Festival
item.description:
Bangladeshi actor Chiranjit Biswas won the Best Male Actor award for his performance in “Delupi” at the 21st Tasveer Film Festival (TFF), held in Seattle, United States. The festival's closing ceremony took place on October 18.
Director Mohammad Touqir Islam attended the ceremony and accepted the award on Biswas's behalf, according to a press release.
Tasveer is an Oscar-qualifying South Asian film festival. “Delupi” was the only Bangladeshi film selected for this year's lineup.
The film is set to compete in the main competition sections of 2 more international festivals on October 24: the 39th Virginia Film Festival in the United States and the London Bridge Film Festival in the United Kingdom.
Produced by Footprint Film Production, “Delupi” draws inspiration from the collapse of a flood embankment in the Khulna region and the political turmoil in Bangladesh in 2024.
Released in Bangladeshi cinemas in 2025, the film has also screened at several international festivals, including the International Film Festival Rotterdam in the Netherlands and Karawan Film Fest in Italy.

item.title: Jubo Dal leader hacked to death in Narayanganj
item.description:
A Jubo Dal leader was hacked to death in Sonargaon upazila of Narayanganj on Wednesday night.
The incident took place in the Char Kishoreganj area around 10pm, said Sonargaon police station Officer-in-Charge Mohammad Abdul Barek.
The deceased, Fakir Zahir Rahman, 40, was the son of Abdur Rahman of Kalapaharia union in neighbouring Araihazar upazila. He was a joint convener of the upazila Jubo Dal and president of the union unit of the organization.
The OC told the media that although Zahir was originally from Araihazar, he had been living in a rented house in Munshiganj Sadar for several years. He also owned a pharmacy in Char Kishoreganj.
Citing preliminary findings, the OC said: “As he did every day, he was returning home after closing his pharmacy on Wednesday night. On the way, unidentified assailants hacked him with sharp weapons and left him injured on the road.”
Local residents later rescued him and took him to Munshiganj General Hospital, where he died while undergoing treatment.
The police official said the body was recovered and sent to the morgue of Narayanganj General Hospital for an autopsy.
The identities of those involved and the motive behind the killing were not immediately known. Police are investigating the incident, the OC added.
